ranges.en: Rabbi Eliezer's position: insert the rain phrase from the first Festival day of Sukkot.
Rabbi Yehoshua's position: insert the rain phrase only from the last Festival day of Sukkot.
Yehoshua objects: rain is a sign of curse during Sukkot, so why mention it then?
Eliezer replies that the phrase is mentioning, not requesting rain, so it is proper at this time.
Yehoshua presses: if mentioning is not requesting, one should always mention rain, even in summer.
General principle: one requests rain only immediately before the rainy season.
Rabbi Yehuda's rule on the prayer leaders at the close of Sukkot versus the first day of Passover.
Where does the tanna stand when he teaches the starting point, given that the obligation is already established?
The tanna relies on a mishna in tractate Berakhot.
Quotes the Berakhot mishna placing rain mentions in the resurrection and blessing of the years, reiterating the starting point.
Why would the tanna defer this halakha to Ta'anit rather than teaching it in Berakhot?
The tanna was interrupted by a discussion in Rosh HaShana, which led him to teach it here.
Quotes the Rosh HaShana mishna stating that on Sukkot all creatures are judged for water.
Explains that the Rosh HaShana mishna's mention of Sukkot judgment prompted the tanna to teach the rain phrase here.
Why not teach simply the starting point for mentioning rains, and what does the phrase 'might of the rains' mean?
Rabbi Yoḥanan: rains are called mighty because they fall with might.
Cites Job 5:9 and 5:10 as scriptural support that rainfall displays God's great, unfathomable works.
From where can it be inferred that these verses present rainfall as a mighty act of God?
Rabba bar Sheila: a verbal analogy with the word 'comprehension' from the account of creation.
Two verses with 'beyond comprehension' and 'girded with might' tie rainfall to creation and divine might.
From where do we know that rain must be requested specifically within the prayer?
Baraita citing Deuteronomy 11:13 about serving God with all one's heart.
The service of the heart is identified as prayer.
Deuteronomy 11:14 follows in juxtaposition, linking rain to the service of the heart.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: God alone holds three keys, rain, birth, and resurrection, never entrusted to an agent.
Cites Deuteronomy 28:12 where God opens the heavens to give rain, supporting the key of rain.
From where is the key of birth derived?
Cites Genesis 30:22 where God remembers Rachel and listens, supporting the key of birth.

ranges.en: Completes the Genesis verse about God opening Rachel's womb as proof that birth is in God's hands.
From where is it derived that the key of resurrection is maintained by God?
Cites Ezekiel 37:13 about God opening the graves, supporting the key of resurrection.
Sages of Eretz Yisrael add a fourth key, the key of livelihood, held by God.
Cites Psalms 145:16 about God opening His hand to satisfy every living thing.
Why did Rabbi Yoḥanan not list the key of livelihood among his keys?
He could have said rain is the same as livelihood, since it is indispensable to all sustenance.
Restates the mishna's position that Rabbi Eliezer says one mentions rain from the first Festival day.
A dilemma: did Rabbi Eliezer derive his ruling from the lulav mitzva or from the water libation?
Cites the teaching that libations may be offered at night, supporting the water-libation derivation.
Resolution: Rabbi Abbahu held the ruling derives from the lulav, learned by tradition or from a baraita.
What is the baraita from which Rabbi Abbahu derived his statement?
Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer says mention rain from taking the lulav; Rabbi Yehoshua says from putting it down.
Rabbi Eliezer's rationale: the four species appear to appease water, as they cannot exist without it.
Rabbi Yehoshua objects that rain during Sukkot is only a sign of a curse.
Rabbi Eliezer replies that he meant mentioning, not requesting, rain, as with resurrection mentioned all year.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: one ceases to mention rain once one ceases to request it.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira: one mentions rain on the second Festival day of Sukkot.
Rabbi Akiva: one mentions rain on the sixth day of Sukkot.
Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua: prayer leaders' rule on the last and first prayer leaders of Sukkot and Passover.
Gemara notes Rabbi Eliezer argued well; how does Rabbi Yehoshua answer his argument?
Rabbi Yehoshua: resurrection is mentioned daily since any day can be its proper time, unlike rain.
But are all times of rainfall its proper time for mentioning it?
Mishna: rain falling after Nisan is a sign of a curse, supported by the verse in Samuel 12:17.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira again: one mentions rain on the second day of Sukkot.
What is the reason for Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's ruling?
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira derives the water libation allusion from the spelling of the libation terms.
What is different about the second day, that Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira chose it?
The allusion to the water libation first appears on the second day, so rain is mentioned from then.
Rabbi Akiva says one mentions rain on the sixth day of Sukkot.
Cites the sixth-day libations verse, read as two libations: one of water and one of wine.
Objection: both libations could be wine, so the verse does not prove a water libation.
Reply: Rabbi Akiva holds with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira that the superfluous letters allude to water.

ranges.en: Objection: if Rabbi Akiva follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, he should say the libation begins on the second day.
Reply: Rabbi Akiva holds the extra libation reference is written regarding the sixth day, indicating a water libation.
Baraita of Rabbi Natan citing Numbers 28:7 with the repeated libation term as evidence of two libations.
The baraita's explanation: the verse speaks of two libations, one of water and one of wine.
Objection: both libations could be of wine, so the verse need not have been written this way.
Reply: the varied wording of the verb teaches that one libation is water and the other is wine.
If a mishna teaches water libation on all seven days, whose opinion is it, and what does each authority imply?
The mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, who holds in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda's ruling.
Mishna of Rabbi Yehuda: he poured water all eight days, removing the first day and adding the eighth.
Why is the first day excluded from water libation, if the allusion logic would also exclude the eighth?
The mishna follows Rabbi Yehoshua, for water libation on all seven days is a halakha learned from tradition.
Rabbi Ami citing Rabbi Yoḥanan: the water libation is a halakha transmitted to Moses at Sinai.
Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua on which prayer leader mentions rain on Sukkot and Passover.
To which Rabbi Yehoshua does the baraita refer, as neither the mishna's nor the baraita's version fits the ruling?
Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda in the name of ben Beteira on the last prayer leader mentioning rain on the Eighth Day.
Which ben Beteira is meant, since Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira ruled that rain is mentioned from the second day?
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: the ben Beteira is Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira, named differently before and after ordination.
Baraita: the Sages did not obligate mentioning dew and wind in the blessing, but one may mention them optionally.
What is the reason the mention of dew and wind is optional?
Rabbi Ḥanina: winds and dew are consistent and never withheld, since the world cannot exist without them.
From where do we learn that dew is not withheld?
Cites I Kings 17:1 and 18:1, where God promised to send rain but Elijah's words mention no dew.
Why did God not mention dew when promising rain to Elijah?

ranges.en: If dew is never withheld, why did Elijah swear there would be no dew as well as no rain?
Elijah meant that even the dew of blessing, which aids crops, would not come.
If so, God should have restored the dew of blessing when ending the drought?
Restoration was unnecessary because the dew of blessing is not recognizable apart from ordinary dew.
From where do we derive that winds are never withheld but always blow?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites Zechariah 2:10, 'as the four winds of heaven', as evidence winds never cease.
What is God telling Israel by saying 'as the four winds', and does it mean scattering them?
Objection: if scattering were meant, the verse should have said 'four in four', not 'as the four winds'.
Rather, God says just as the world cannot exist without winds, it cannot exist without the Jewish people.
Rabbi Ḥanina's rulings on whether to repeat the wind and rain blessings in summer and in the rainy season.
Baraita: the Sages did not obligate mentioning clouds and winds, but one may mention them optionally.
What is the reason that clouds and winds are not obligatory, since they are not withheld?
Baraita of Rav Yosef on Deuteronomy 11:17 shows heaven is closed off from clouds and winds, so they can be withheld.
The baraitot appear to contradict each other on winds and on clouds.
Clouds differ: early clouds come before rain regardless, while late clouds after rain may be withheld.
Winds differ: a typical wind is never withheld, while an atypical wind may be withheld.
An atypical wind is useful for winnowing grain, so should one pray for it too?
Winnowing with sieves is possible without wind, so these winds are not greatly needed.
Baraita: clouds and winds are second in benefit only to rain.
Ulla, or Rav Yehuda: the baraita refers to clouds and winds that come after rainfall.
Objection: the Deuteronomy curse of rain turning to dust suggests post-rain winds are harmful, not beneficial.
Ulla: gentle post-rain wind is beneficial, while forceful wind raising dust harms rain's effect.
Rav Yehuda: post-rain wind, clouds, and sun are as beneficial as rain, sun even as two rainfalls.
What does Rav Yehuda's statement serve to exclude?
It excludes evening glow and sun shining in patches between clouds, which harm after rain.
Rava: snow benefits mountains as much as five rainfalls benefit the plains.
Cites Job 37:6, with repeated rain terms, as allusion to five types of rainfall, supporting snow's value.
Rava: snow benefits mountains, strong rain benefits trees, and light rain benefits fruit.

ranges.en: Rava's image: a gentle drizzle benefits a seed under a clod of earth without harming it.
What is the meaning of the word 'urpila', drizzle?
It is a contraction of the phrase 'Arise, furrows', i.e., uru pilei.
Rava: a Torah scholar is like a seed under a clod, growing and increasing in greatness once he sprouts.
Rava: a Torah scholar who grows angry is presumably angered by his own Torah study, so he deserves the benefit of the doubt.
Cites Jeremiah 23:29, 'Is not My word like fire,' to support the fiery nature of Torah.
Rav Ashi: a Torah scholar who is not hard as iron, but wavers, is not a Torah scholar.
Cites Jeremiah 23:29, 'like a hammer that breaks rock,' to support Rav Ashi's view.
Rabbi Abba objects: Rav Ashi should have learned this from a different verse, not from Jeremiah.
Cites Deuteronomy 8:9, reading 'avaneha' as 'boneha', showing Torah scholars build the land and are iron-hard.
Ravina: even so, one must teach himself to act gently and not be harsh.
Cites Ecclesiastes 11:10, 'remove anger from your heart,' as support for Ravina's gentleness.
Rabbi Yonatan's teaching: three people asked God unreasonably; two got reasonable answers and one an unreasonable answer.
Eliezer, Abraham's servant, asked for a sign in Genesis 24:14, which was answered fittingly by Rebecca.
Eliezer's request was unreasonable since it allowed even a lame or blind woman, yet God answered fittingly.
Cites I Samuel 17:25, Saul's offer to enrich whoever kills Goliath and marry him to his daughter.
Saul's offer was unreasonable since it allowed even a slave or mamzer, yet God answered fittingly with David.
Cites Judges 11:31, Jephthah's vow to offer whatever comes out of his house as a burnt offering.
Jephthah's vow was unreasonable since it could include an impure animal, yet God answered unreasonably with his daughter.
Cites Jeremiah 8:22, 'Is there no balm in Gilead,' which alludes to Jephthah being able to annul his vow.
Cites Jeremiah 19:5 on child sacrifice, 'which I did not command, nor did it come into My heart.'
Interprets the verse: 'which I did not command' refers to the son of Mesha, king of Moab.
Cites II Kings 3:27, where Mesha offered his firstborn son as a burnt offering.
Interprets 'nor did it come into My heart' as Isaac, whose sacrifice was only a test and not God's intent.
Rabbi Berekhya: the Congregation of Israel also asked unreasonably, yet God answered fittingly.
Cites Hosea 6:3, 'He will come to us as the rain,' comparing God's revelation to rain.
God replies: rain is sometimes desired and sometimes not, so I will be like the always desired dew.
Cites Hosea 14:6, 'I will be as the dew to Israel,' supporting dew as always a blessing.
The Congregation of Israel again asked unreasonably, requesting God be a seal upon the heart and arm.
Cites Song of Songs 8:6, 'Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm.'
God replies: I will manifest Myself as something always visible, not something sometimes seen.
Cites Isaiah 49:16, 'Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of My hands,' as God's constant visibility.
Restates the mishna's principle that one requests rain only near the start of the rainy season.
The Sages assumed requesting and mentioning rain are one matter; who is the tanna who taught this?
Rava: it is Rabbi Yehoshua, who holds one mentions rain from putting down the lulav.
Abaye: even per Rabbi Eliezer, requesting and mentioning are distinct, so requests start only just before the rainy season.
Another version of the discussion opens with a proposed reading, cut off at the daf's end.

ranges.en: Restates that the mishna follows Rabbi Yehoshua, who says one mentions rain from putting the lulav down.
Rava: even if the mishna follows Rabbi Eliezer, requesting and mentioning are distinct, so the rule still holds.
Mishna of Rabbi Yehuda on prayer leaders on the Eighth Day of Assembly and on the first day of Passover.
Contradiction from a baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says request rain until Passover ends, but the mishna implies an earlier end.
Rav Ḥisda: no contradiction; the baraita speaks of requesting until Passover ends, the mishna of mentioning until the first day.
Ulla: Rav Ḥisda's resolution is unacceptable, since one who mentions when not requesting should also mention when requesting.
Ulla's alternative: two tanna'im hold different rulings in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Yosef: 'until Passover has passed' means until the first prayer leader descends to pray on the first day.
Abaye asks: is there a request for rain on a Festival, when the ninth blessing is not recited?
Rav Yosef: the baraita refers to a translator's rain request after the prayers; Ulla's two-tanna'im view is clearer.
Rabba: 'until Passover has passed' means until the slaughter time of the Paschal lamb, so mention continues one day longer.
Abaye objects: mention at the start has appeasement value, but at the end there is no request to appease.
Rabbi Asi, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan: the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Zeira objects: a mishna says request starts on the third or seventh of Marḥeshvan, and Rabbi Elazar ruled per Rabban Gamliel.
Rabbi Asi: contradicting one man with another is unfounded; request and mention are distinct, resolving the apparent conflict.
Does Rabbi Yoḥanan's rule that mention accompanies request conflict with his statement about starting and ceasing?
Babylonians and Eretz Yisrael differ: Babylonians have fruit in the field, while Eretz Yisrael has pilgrims travelling home.
Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling refers to the period without the Temple, so the two statements apply to different periods.
How do Diaspora Jews, with two Festival days, handle the start of rain mention given the uncertain Eighth Day?
Rav: begin mentioning rain at the Eighth Day's additional prayer, pause for the next day's services, then resume at Simḥat Torah.
Shmuel objects: once the first day of the Eighth Day is sanctified, one should not treat it as a non-Festival day.
Shmuel's own ruling: begin in additional and afternoon prayers, pause for evening and morning, and resume at Simḥat Torah.

ranges.en: Rava offers an alternative view: once one starts mentioning rain, he never stops until summer.
Rav Sheshet holds the same rule that once one starts mentioning rain he does not stop.
The Gemara notes that Rav himself retracted his earlier position.
Rav's earlier view, as reported by Rav Hananel: count twenty-one days from Rosh HaShana before starting the rain mention.
The Gemara concludes that the halakha follows the rule that once one starts mentioning rain he does not stop.
The Mishnah opens by asking until when one requests rain.
Rabbi Yehuda says rain is requested until Passover has passed.
Rabbi Meir says rain is requested until the month of Nisan has ended.
A verse from Joel says rain falls in the first month, supporting Rabbi Meir that Nisan is part of the rainy season.
Rav Naḥman challenges Rabbi Yitzḥak: rain does not fall in Nisan, since the first rain is in Marḥeshvan.
A mishnah teaches that the first rain falls in Marḥeshvan and the late rain in Nisan, supporting the objection.
Rabbi Yoḥanan replies that the verse about rain in Nisan was fulfilled in the days of Joel.
Rabbi Yoḥanan cites Joel's description of locust devastation as the year in question.
That year Adar ended without rain, and the first rain fell on the first of Nisan, upholding Rabbi Meir.
A prophet tells the people to go out and sow.
The people object: a person with little grain should eat it and live, not sow it and die.
The prophet replies that they should sow regardless.
A miracle followed: hidden seeds were found, and a second rain fell on the fifth of Nisan.
The people brought the omer offering on the sixteenth of Nisan.
The crop that normally grows in six months grew in eleven days, so the omer came from eleven-day grain.
A verse from Psalms about sowing in tears and reaping in joy is cited as describing that generation.
What is the meaning of the phrase about going forth weeping and bearing the measure of seed?
Rabbi Yehuda explains that the ox plowed weeping, then ate sprouts on its return, so the verse describes joy at harvest.
What is the meaning of the phrase about bearing his sheaves?
Rav Ḥisda, citing a baraita, says the stalk was one span and the ear two spans, an unusually large yield.
Rav Naḥman asks what the people ate during the seven years of famine described in Kings.
Rabbi Yoḥanan explains the seven years: houses, fields, then kosher and non-kosher animals, then creeping things, children, and finally their own arms.
The final stage is said to fulfill the verse in Isaiah that each man eats the flesh of his own arm.
Rav Naḥman asks how to understand the verse in Hosea that the holy one is in your midst so God will not enter the city.
Rabbi Yoḥanan explains that God will not enter the heavenly Jerusalem until entering the earthly Jerusalem.
Does a Jerusalem exist above in heaven?
Yes, the Gemara answers affirmatively.
A verse from Psalms describing Jerusalem as a city joined together is cited as proof of a heavenly counterpart.
What is the meaning of the verse in Jeremiah describing the foolish being taught vanity, which is wood?
Rabbi Yoḥanan says one sin sends the wicked to Gehenna.
What is that sin?
That sin is idol worship.
A verbal analogy links the word vanity in two Jeremiah verses, proving the idolatry reading.
Rav Naḥman asks about the verse saying two evils were done, when the Gemara counts more than two.
Rabbi Yoḥanan answers that they committed only one sin, which is the one that counts.

ranges.en: The sin of idolatry is equal in weight to two other sins.
What exactly is that sin?
The sin is idol worship.
A verse in Jeremiah describing the people forsaking the living waters for broken cisterns is cited.
A second Jeremiah verse about nations exchanging their gods for what does not profit is cited.
A baraita teaches that Kittites worship fire and Kedarites worship water.
Even knowing water extinguishes fire, they did not exchange their god, which the verse condemns Israel for doing.
How could Samuel be called old at a young death age of fifty-two?
Rabbi Yoḥanan says old age came upon Samuel early, making him look older than he was.
A verse in Samuel records God regretting making Saul king.
Samuel pleads before God that he should be treated like Moses and Aaron.
A verse in Psalms lists Moses, Aaron, and Samuel together as those who call upon God.
Samuel argues that just as Moses and Aaron's work was not annulled in their lifetimes, neither should his be.
God asks what to do: should Saul die now?
Samuel's petition prevents Saul's death, and Samuel cannot die early either, since the time of David has come.
Kingdoms do not overlap or subtract time from one another, not even by a hairbreadth.
God therefore decides to bring old age upon Samuel so people will think he is elderly.
A verse says Saul dwelled in Gibeah under a tree in Rama, supporting the idea that Samuel's prayer affected Saul.
What does Gibeah have to do with Rama, since they are separate places?
The verse teaches that Samuel's prayer from Rama caused Saul to remain in Gibeah for two and a half years.
Is one man set aside before another man?
Yes, Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said so.
Rabbi Yoḥanan cites a Hosea verse where God slays prophets by the words of His mouth, not by their deeds.
The conclusion: one man is indeed set aside before another.
Rav Naḥman and Rabbi Yitzḥak were sitting together at a meal.
Rav Naḥman asks Rabbi Yitzḥak to share a teaching with him.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says one should not speak during a meal, lest food enter the windpipe and cause choking.
Rabbi Yitzḥak claims that Rabbi Yoḥanan held that our patriarch Jacob did not die.
Rav Naḥman objects that the mourners eulogized, embalmed, and buried him, so he must have died.
Rabbi Yitzḥak replies that he is interpreting a verse.
A Jeremiah verse promises Jacob's seed will be saved, and describes them as alive.
The verse equates Jacob with his seed, so just as the seed is alive, Jacob is alive.
Rabbi Yitzḥak says whoever says Rahab Rahab immediately experiences seminal emission.
Rav Naḥman says he says Rahab and it does not affect him.
Rabbi Yitzḥak clarifies he meant someone who knew her personally or recognized her.
The two parted from one another.
Rav Naḥman asks Rabbi Yitzḥak for a blessing.
Rabbi Yitzḥak offers to tell him a parable.
A parable describes a hungry traveler in the desert who finds a tree with sweet fruit, pleasant shade, and flowing water.
When the traveler wants to leave, he says he will bless the tree.
With what shall I bless you, tree?
The tree already has sweet fruit, pleasant shade, and flowing water, so these blessings are unnecessary.
Instead the traveler blesses that all saplings planted from the tree should be like it.

ranges.en: Rabbi Yitzhak's blessing: may you be like this tree.
With what shall I bless you?
You already have Torah, wealth, and children, so those blessings are unnecessary.
Rather, the blessing is that your descendants will be like you.
A baraita: the first rain is named yoreh because it instructs people to prepare roofs and harvests.
An alternative explanation: yoreh moistens the earth down to its depths.
A Psalms verse about soft showers blessing the growth is cited for that alternative.
Another alternative: yoreh falls gently rather than with violence.
The Gemara raises the opposite reading: yoreh strips fruit, washes away seeds and trees.
The word malkosh is compared to yoreh to show both are rains for blessing.
The opposite reading of malkosh: a destructive rain that knocks down houses and trees.
The word yoreh is compared to malkosh to show that the destructive reading is rejected.
From where do we derive that yoreh itself is a blessing?
A verse in Joel says God gave the yoreh for righteousness, showing the first rain is a blessing.
A baraita: the first rain falls in Marheshvan and the last rain in Nisan.
Do you say the first rain is in Marheshvan and the last in Nisan?
Or perhaps the first rain is in Tishrei and the last rain in Iyyar.
The verse says the rain comes in its time, which settles the matter.
Rav Nehilai bar Idi, citing Shmuel, says malkosh subdues the stubbornness of the Jewish people.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael says malkosh fills out the grain in its stalks.
A baraita says malkosh falls on the ears and the stalks.
A baraita repeats that the first rain falls in Marheshvan and the last in Nisan.
Do you say the first rain is in Marheshvan?
Or perhaps it is only in Kislev.
The verse says in its time for both rains, so the first rain also falls in its proper time.
Parenthetically: once Nisan has passed and rain falls, it is not a sign of blessing.
Rabbi Meir says the first rain is in Marheshvan, while the Rabbis say it is in Kislev.
Who are the Rabbis mentioned here?
Rav Hisda says it is the opinion of Rabbi Yosei.
A baraita: Rabbi Meir gives the earliest, intermediate, and latest dates for the first rainfall as the third, seventh, and seventeenth of Marheshvan.
Rabbi Yehuda gives the seventh, seventeenth, and twenty-third of Marheshvan.
Rabbi Yosei gives the seventeenth, twenty-third, and New Moon of Kislev.
Rabbi Yosei adds that individuals do not begin a drought fast before the New Moon of Kislev.
Rav Hisda rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
Ameimar taught Rav Hisda's ruling as beginning to request rain on the third of Marheshvan.
Rabban Gamliel says one begins requesting rain on the seventh of Marheshvan.
Rav Hisda rules that the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel.
In accordance with whose opinion is the following baraita?
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says rains falling seven consecutive days count as the first rainfall, and a count of rainfalls follows.
In accordance with whose opinion are the second and third rainfalls counted?
It is in accordance with Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Hisda says the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
Granted the first and third rainfalls matter, but why is the second rainfall mentioned?
Rabbi Zeira says the second rainfall matters for the laws of vows, as taught in a mishna.
