ranges.en: A vow prohibiting benefit until the rains lasts until the second rainfall, which counts as the rainy season.
Rav Zevid says the second rainfall also matters for the laws of olive gleaning.
A mishna on gleaning rules says forgotten olives may be taken only after the second rainfall.
What does the term namoshot, searchers, mean?
Rabbi Yoḥanan says they are elders who walk slowly with a staff, so they see everything.
Reish Lakish says they are gleaners who come after all the other gleaners.
Rav Pappa says the second rainfall matters for when one may walk on permitted paths through fields.
A teaching says anyone may use permitted paths until the second rainfall, since later walking damages crops.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak says the second rainfall matters for removing Sabbatical produce.
A mishna says straw and hay of the Sabbatical may be used until the second rainfall.
What is the reason Sabbatical produce must be removed from the house?
Leviticus says beasts may eat from the field, so household feed must stop once the field no longer provides it.
What is the meaning of the term revia for rainfall?
Revia means rain that penetrates and fructifies the earth, following Rav Yehuda's view that rain is the husband of the earth.
Isaiah compares rain that waters the earth and makes it sprout to a husband and wife.
Rabbi Abbahu says first rain must soak a handbreadth into the ground, and second rain must seal a barrel's opening with mud.
Rav Ḥisda says rain that seals a barrel's opening does not fulfill the verse about the heavens closing.
Rav Ḥisda says rain falling before the Shema, even if it does not continue, is not an instance of closing the heavens.
Abaye limits this: only rain before the evening Shema counts, while morning rain may still count.
Rav Yehuda bar Yitzḥak says morning clouds have no substance.
Hosea compares Judah's goodness to a morning cloud, showing morning clouds bring little benefit.
Rav Pappa objects that people say morning rain at the doors means rain all day.
The Gemara answers: the two statements refer to heavy clouds versus light clouds.
Rav Yehuda says it is good for the year when Tevet has no rain.
Two explanations are given for why no rain in Tevet is good: to avoid desolate gardens, and to avoid blight.
Rav Ḥisda says that rain in Tevet being muddy is good, which seems to contradict Rav Yehuda.
The conflict is resolved: one case had rain earlier, the other did not.
Rav Ḥisda says rain falling on part of a country but not another does not fulfill the verse about closing the heavens.
The Gemara objects with Amos, where God withheld rain from one city and rained on another, which is a curse.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, says both the rained-on and unrained-on areas are cursed.
The contradiction is resolved: excess rain in one area is a curse, while the needed amount is a blessing.
Rav Ashi says the verse in Amos uses the phrase making a place of rain, showing this reading is correct.
Rabbi Abbahu says one begins to bless on rain when the groom goes out to meet the bride, i.e., when puddles form.
What blessing does one recite over rain?
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, gives the blessing thanking God for each and every drop.
Rabbi Yoḥanan adds to the blessing with a longer formula of praise, concluding with the nishmat-style closing.
Why does the blessing say abundant thanksgivings rather than all thanksgivings?
Rava says to emend the wording to God of thanksgivings.
Rav Pappa says since opinions differ on this, the matter remains unsettled.

7a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Instruction to recite both thanksgiving formulations, God of thanksgivings and abundant thanksgivings.
Rabbi Abbahu holds rain surpasses resurrection, since rain benefits both righteous and wicked.
Rav Yosef disagrees: rain equals resurrection, which is why the Sages placed it in the resurrection blessing.
Rav Yehuda holds the day of rains is as great as the day the Torah was given.
Deuteronomy and Proverbs verses, reading lekah as Torah, support comparing rain to the giving of Torah.
Rava holds rain exceeds the day of Torah's giving, since the lesser is dependent on the greater.
Rava notes a contradiction: the same verses describe the teaching as harsh rain and as gentle dew.
Resolution: a worthy scholar receives Torah like dew, while an unworthy one is snapped like rain.
Baraita: Torah study for its own sake becomes an elixir of life for the student.
Proverbs verses describe Torah as a tree of life, healing, and life for those who find wisdom.
Torah study not for its own sake becomes an elixir of death for the student.
Verses on rain and on breaking the heifer's neck show that arifa means killing.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira to teach a halakhic discourse.
Rabbi Zeira declines, saying he is too weak to deliver a halakhic discourse.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks instead for a teaching of aggada.
Rabbi Zeira reports a teaching of Rabbi Yohanan on the aggada.
What does the verse comparing man to a tree of the field mean, since a man is not a tree?
Trees may be cut only when the scholar is unworthy, read from the verse distinguishing eating from destroying.
Rabbi Hama son of Rabbi Hanina teaches in the name of Rabbi Hanina.
Proverbs verse on iron sharpening iron is cited as a source.
Just as iron sharpens iron, Torah scholars studying together sharpen one another in halakha.
Why are matters of Torah compared to fire?
Jeremiah verse: Is not My word like fire, says the Lord.
As a lone stick does not burn, Torah matters are not retained by a solitary student.
Introduces Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina's teaching on the same point.
Asks what a verse in Jeremiah means.
Homiletic reading: the sword falls on enemies of scholars who sit alone and study Torah solitarily.
Solitary study does not only fail to sharpen; it makes one foolish.
Quotes the word noalu from the same verse as proof of foolishness.
Solitary study leads not only to folly but to sin.
Compares the word noalu in Jeremiah with the wording in Numbers, noalnu and chatanu.
Alternative source: Isaiah's princes of Zoan who became fools and led Egypt astray.
Why are matters of Torah likened to a tree?
Proverbs verse calls Torah a tree of life for those who hold fast to it.
As a small piece of wood kindles a large one, minor scholars sharpen great ones.
Rabbi Hanina: he learned much from teachers, more from peers, and most from students.
Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa raises a contradiction between two verses about water for the thirsty.
Isaiah verses: bring water to the thirsty, and everyone who thirsts come for water.
If the student is worthy the teacher must seek him out; otherwise the student must seek the teacher.
Rabbi Hanina bar Hama raises a contradiction between dispersing springs and keeping them for oneself.
Proverbs verses: let your springs be dispersed abroad, and let them be your own.
If the student is worthy, disperse your teaching; if not, keep it for yourself.
Rabbi Hanina bar Idi asks why Torah is likened to water.
Isaiah verse: everyone who thirsts, come for water.
As water flows from high to low, Torah is retained only by one with a humble spirit.
Rabbi Oshaya asks why Torah is likened to water, wine and milk.
Isaiah verses cite water, and buying wine and milk without money.
As these liquids keep only in lowly vessels, Torah is retained only by one who is humble.
The emperor's daughter remarks that wisdom in an ugly vessel is a pity.
Yehoshua answers with a deflecting question about where the emperor keeps his wine.
The daughter asks in what vessel the wine should then be kept.
Yehoshua tells her to keep wine in gold and silver vessels.
The daughter relays the advice; the wine soured in gold and silver, and the advisors report it.
The emperor asks who told his daughter to do this.
The daughter names Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya.
The emperor asks Yehoshua why he said this to her.
Yehoshua says he answered her as she had answered him, to show fine things keep best in plain vessels.
The emperor objects that there are handsome people who are learned.

7b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Yehoshua replies that had the sages been ugly, they would have been even more learned.
Alternative explanation: like liquids, Torah is spoiled and forgotten only through diversion of attention.
Rabbi Hama bar Hanina: the day of rains is as great as the day heaven and earth were created.
Isaiah verse on the heavens pouring righteousness, with the phrase I the Lord created it.
The verse uses the singular form bera'tiv, not the plural, which is the point being made.
Rav Oshaya: the day of rains is so great that salvation is multiplied through it.
Isaiah verse: let the earth open and let salvation sprout.
Rabbi Tanhum bar Hanilai: rains fall only once Israel's sins have been forgiven.
Psalm verse: You forgave the iniquity of your people and covered all their sins.
Ze'iri rebukes Ravina: you learn this point from one verse, and we learn it from another.
Kings verse: hear from heaven and forgive the sin, offered as the source Ze'iri's school uses.
Rabbi Tanhum, son of Rabbi Hiyya of Kfar Akko: rains are withheld only when Israel's enemies are doomed.
Job verse on drought and heat taking the waters of snow, cited as support.
Ze'iri again disputes the source with Ravina, each side citing a different verse.
Deuteronomy verse: the heavens are shut up and you perish quickly.
Rav Hisda: rains are withheld only because of neglect of terumot and ma'aserot.
Job verse on drought and heat taking the waters of snow.
What does this verse indicate?
A Tanna of Rabbi Yishmael's school: rain is withheld for not observing commandments in the summer.
Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi: rains are withheld only because of gossipers and those who speak evil.
Proverbs verse: a north wind brings rain, and a hidden tongue brings angry faces.
Rav Sala, citing Rav Hamnuna: rains are withheld only because of brazen faces.
Jeremiah verse: showers were withheld, and you have the forehead of a harlot.
Rav Sala, citing Rav Hamnuna: anyone with a brazen face ends up stumbling into sin.
Jeremiah verse about the forehead of a harlot, cited as support for the claim that brazenness leads to sin.
Rav Naḥman: it is known that one with a brazen face stumbles into sin.
Jeremiah verse, read by its wording as having a harlot's forehead, cited to show that the sin is known.
Rabba bar Rav Huna: one with a brazen face may be called wicked.
Proverbs verse: the wicked man hardens his face.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: one may hate such a person.
Ecclesiastes verse: his brazen face is hated.
Do not read the verb as yishune but as yisna, a textual correction.
Rav Ketina: rains are withheld only because of neglect of Torah study.
Ecclesiastes verse: through laziness the roof sags.
Explains the verse: laziness among Israel who did not study Torah makes God their enemy.
The word makh means only a poor person.
Leviticus verse: if he is poor, and his valuation is set.
Makreh means only the Holy One, blessed be He.
Psalm verse: he lays the beams of his chambers in the waters.
Rav Yosef: learn it from here.
Job verse: now no one sees the bright light in the skies, but wind passes and clears them.
Light means only Torah.
Proverbs verse: the commandment is a lamp and the Torah is a bright light.
Baraita of Rabbi Yishmael's school: even when the sky is made of bronze, rain and dew are sent down.
Rabbi Ami: rains are withheld only because of the sin of robbery.
Job verse: he covers the light with his hands and commands it to strike.
Hands here means only violence.
Jonah verse: the violence that is in their hands.
Light here means only rain.
Job verse: he scatters the cloud with his light.
What is the remedy?
One should increase prayer.
Job verse: he commanded it by intercession.
Intercession here means only prayer.
Jeremiah verse: do not pray for this people, and do not intercede with me.
Rabbi Ami asks what the verse in Ecclesiastes means.
Ecclesiastes verse: if the iron is blunt and one does not sharpen its edge.
If you see the sky as blunt as iron, it withholds rain because of the generation's corrupt deeds.
The verse: and he did not sharpen its edge.
What is their remedy?
They should strengthen themselves through compassion.
Ecclesiastes verse: strength will prevail through wisdom.
The verse's logic: if wisdom is made fit, how much more so are the deeds of those made fit from the start.
Resh Lakish opens a conditional teaching about what one sees in a student, continuing past this daf.

8a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Resh Lakish continues: a student whose learning is hard as iron, because his teacher does not order his teaching for him.
What is the remedy for such a student?
He should increase his study in the yeshiva, based on the Ecclesiastes verse about strength prevailing.
By kal vachomer: if wisdom is made fit by such study, how much more so one whose learning was ordered from the start.
Resh Lakish used to arrange the Mishnah forty times, corresponding to the forty days of the giving of the Torah.
Rav Adda bar Ahava arranged the Mishnah twenty-four times, corresponding to Torah, Prophets, and Writings.
Narrates that the same student went before Rava.
Rava: if a student's learning is hard as iron because his teacher does not show him a friendly face.
Ecclesiastes verse: and he did not sharpen its edge.
What is the remedy for this student?
He should increase companions around him.
Ecclesiastes verse on strength prevailing and wisdom being made fit.
Kal vachomer: if he was made fit by his teacher's face, how much more so from the start.
Rabbi Ami asks what the Ecclesiastes verse on the snake and the whisperer means.
Ecclesiastes verse: if the snake bites without whispering, the whisperer has no advantage.
Explains that a generation whose sky is like brass withholds rain because of incantation-whisperers.
What is the remedy in that case?
People should go to one who knows how to whisper.
Job verse: his fellow tells him of it.
Continuation of the verse: the whisperer has no advantage.
One who can whisper but does not, gets no benefit; if he whispered and was not answered, the same applies.
What is the remedy for this case?
He should go to a pious man in the generation and increase prayer on his behalf.
Job verse: he commanded it by intercession.
Intercession here means only prayer.
Jeremiah verse: do not pray for this people, and do not lift up cry or prayer for them, nor intercede with Me.
If the whisper succeeds, arrogance brings it upon the one who whispered, forever.
Job verse: it declares concerning it, the cattle also, concerning the ascending sacrifice.
Rava: two Torah scholars in one city who do not get along in halakha envy each other and raise each other up.
Job verse: the cattle also, concerning the ascending sacrifice.
Resh Lakish asks what the Ecclesiastes verse means.
Ecclesiastes verse: if the snake bites without whispering, the whisperer has no advantage.
In the future all animals gather before the snake and mock it, and it has no advantage in whispering.
Rabbi Ami: a person's prayer is heard only if he places his soul in his palm.
Lamentations verse: let us lift up our hearts with our hands to God.
Is that so? But surely Shmuel the Amora taught otherwise.
Shmuel the Amora taught the verse differently, reading the Psalm on it.
Psalm verse: they deceived Him with their mouths and with their tongues, but their heart was not steadfast.
Psalm verse: yet He is compassionate and forgives iniquity.
No contradiction: one refers to an individual, the other to the community.
Rabbi Ami: rains fall only for the sake of those who are faithful.
Psalm verse: truth springs from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven.
Rabbi Ami: come and see how great the faithful are.
From where is this known?
Kal vachomer from the mole and the pit: one who trusts a mole and a pit, how much more one who trusts God.
Rabbi Yohanan: whoever justifies himself below, judgment is justified for him from above.
Psalm verse: truth springs from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Avin said in the name of Rav Huna, citing a verse.
Psalm verse: as Your fear is, so is Your wrath.
Resh Lakish says it is derived from this verse.
Isaiah verse: You meet him who rejoices and does righteousness; in Your ways they remember You, though You were angry and we sinned.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: whoever rejoices in the sufferings that come upon him brings salvation forever.
Isaiah verse: in them we shall be saved forever.
Resh Lakish said.
What is the meaning of the verse in Deuteronomy?
Deuteronomy verse: the heavens are shut up, so there is no rain.
When the heavens are shut and withhold rain and dew, it is like a woman who miscarries and does not give birth.
This is what Resh Lakish said in the name of Bar Kappara: drought is stated regarding rain, and drought is stated regarding a woman.

8b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Bar Kappara's analogy continues: drought is stated in regard to a woman.
Genesis verse: for the Lord had closed up every womb, cited as the source for the woman analogy.
Drought is also stated in regard to rain.
Deuteronomy verse: the heavens are shut up, cited for the rain side of the analogy.
Birth is stated in regard to a woman and also in regard to rain.
Genesis verse: she conceived and bore a son, cited for the woman side.
Birth is also stated in regard to rain.
Isaiah verse: it brings forth and makes to bud, cited for the rain side.
Remembering is stated in regard to a woman and also in regard to rain.
Genesis verse: the Lord remembered Sarah, cited for the woman side.
Remembering is also stated in regard to rain.
Psalm verse: You remember the earth and water it, cited for the rain side and the stream of God.
What is the meaning of the stream of God being full of water?
Some teach there is a dome-like vessel in the sky from which the rains emerge.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani explains the verse that follows.
What is the meaning of the Job verse?
Job verse: whether for a rod, for the land, or for kindness, rain comes to lands, fields, pits, and springs.
In the days of Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani there was famine and death.
They asked what they should do.
They concluded they had no choice but to pray for mercy and bear the famine.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani says they should pray about hunger, since God gives satiety to the living.
Psalm verse: You open Your hand and satisfy every living thing with favor.
How do we know that one should not pray for the other?
Ezra verse: we fasted and sought our God for this.
This implies there is another view.
In the West they say in the name of Rabbi Haggai that this is derived from another source.
Daniel verse: that they should seek mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery.
This implies there is another view.
In the days of Rabbi Zeira, a decree was issued that one should not sit in fast.
Rabbi Zeira says: we will accept it upon ourselves, and when the decree is annulled we will sit.
They asked him where he got this from.
He told them, as it is written.
Daniel verse: Fear not, Daniel, since from the first day you set your heart to understand and humble yourself before God.
Rabbi Yitzḥak: even two like the two of Elijah, when rain falls on Sabbath eves, are merely a sign of a curse.
Rabba bar Shila: the day of rain is as hard as the day of judgment.
Amemar: if we need a baraita, we pray and annul it.
Rabbi Yitzḥak: the sun on the Sabbath is charity for the poor.
Malachi verse: the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing for those who fear My name.
Rabbi Yitzḥak: the day of rain is great, since even a small coin in the purse is blessed by it.
Deuteronomy verse: the Lord will open His good treasure, to give rain on your land in its season and bless all your work.
Rabbi Yitzḥak: blessing is found only in what is hidden from the eye.
Deuteronomy verse: the Lord will command the blessing upon your storehouses.
A tanna of Rabbi Yishmael's school: blessing is found only in what the eye does not control.
Deuteronomy verse: the Lord will command the blessing upon your storehouses.
A baraita: one who enters to thresh and prays for blessing on his produce, but who blesses before measuring, offers a vain prayer.
A mnemonic list of the four topics the day of rain is compared to.
Rabbi Yohanan: the day of rain is as great as the day of the gathering of exiles.
Psalm verse: restore our captivity, Lord, like the streams in the Negev.
Streams here means only rain.
Samuel verse: the channels of the sea appeared.
Rabbi Yohanan: the day of rain is great, since even troops cease upon it.
Psalm verse: You water its furrows and soften it with showers.
Rabbi Yohanan: rains are withheld only because of those who withhold charity from the public, and do not give.
Proverbs verse: clouds and wind without rain, so a man who boasts of a false gift.
Rabbi Yohanan asks what is the meaning of the verse.

9a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Deuteronomy verse: you shall surely tithe, so that you become wealthy.
Rabbi Yohanan encounters a young student of Resh Lakish and speaks to him.
Rabbi Yohanan asks the boy to tell him his verses.
The boy recites: you shall surely tithe.
Rabbi Yohanan asks what the repeated tithing phrase means.
The boy explains: tithe in order that you become wealthy.
Rabbi Yohanan asks where the boy got this.
The boy tells him to go and test God in this matter.
Objection: may one test God? Surely it is written, you shall not test the Lord.
The boy replies that Rabbi Hoshaya taught an exception for this verse, citing Malachi.
Malachi verse: bring the full tithe into the storehouse, test Me now, and I will open the windows of heaven.
What is the meaning of until there is no more sufficiency?
Until your lips are worn out from saying enough.
Rabbi Yohanan says that had he reached this verse earlier, he would not need the boy or his teacher Rabbi Hoshaya.
Rabbi Yohanan later finds Resh Lakish's student sitting and teaching.
Proverbs verse: a man's folly perverts his way, and his heart rages against the Lord.
Rabbi Yohanan sits and wonders at this.
Rabbi Yohanan asks: is there anything in the Writings that is not hinted at in the Torah?
The boy replies that this one is hinted at, and asks whether a verse in Genesis has not been cited.
Genesis verse: their hearts sank, and they said to one another, what is this God has done to us.
The boy explains the verse through an anecdote about a mother warning her son not to do as his father did.
Rabbi Yohanan: rain comes for the sake of an individual, while sustenance comes for the sake of the many.
Deuteronomy verse: the Lord will open His good treasure to give rain to your land.
Sustenance comes for the sake of the many.
Exodus verse: behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you.
Objection from a baraita: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says three good leaders arose for Israel, Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.
Good gifts were given through them.
The well, the cloud, and the manna were given by the merit of Miriam, Aaron, and Moses respectively.
Numbers verse: Miriam died there and was buried there.
The water returned by the merit of both, since the verse goes on that there was no water for the congregation.
When Aaron died, the clouds of glory departed.
Numbers verse: the Canaanite king of Arad heard that Israel was coming, and thought he had permission to fight Israel.
Numbers verse: all the congregation saw that Aaron had died.
Rabbi Abbahu: do not read the word as vayiru but as vayiru in the sense Resh Lakish taught.
Resh Lakish's principle: the root has four senses, and the verse should be read accordingly.
Both returned by Moses's merit, and when Moses died all departed.
Zechariah verse: I cut off the three shepherds in one month.
Objection: did they all die in one month? Miriam died in Nisan, Aaron in Av, and Moses in Adar.
It teaches that the three good gifts given through them were cancelled and all departed in one month.
Sustenance for an individual is different for Moses, since he was needed by the many and is like the many.
Narrative: students of Rava gathered before Rav Pappa after Rava died, and whenever he taught them a teaching that did not seem sound, they hinted to one another, and he was saddened.

9b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Zechariah verse: I cut off the three shepherds in one month, cited about the dream reading.
Next day, as they were leaving, he told the Rabbis to go, saying that matters were settled.
Narrative: Rav Shimi bar Ashi, who often sat before Rav Pappa and asked him much, once saw a man fall on his face and heard him pray for mercy.
Resh Lakish also holds that rain comes for the sake of an individual.
How do we know that rain comes for the sake of an individual?
Zechariah verse: ask the Lord for rain in the season of the late rain; the Lord makes the storms, and gives rain to each man grass in the field.
Yachol would mean all; Scripture says to a man, so the derivation is limited.
A baraita: yachol would mean all his fields; Scripture says field, and then grass limits it.
Narrative: Rav Daniel bar Katina had a garden; he would walk through it, saying one plot needs water and another does not, until rain fell and watered every place that needed it.
What is the meaning of the Psalm phrase the Lord makes the storms?
Rabbi Yose bar Hanina: this teaches that the Holy One makes a separate storm for each righteous person.
What are the storms?
Rav Yehuda: blossoms.
Rabbi Yohanan: blossoming is a sign of rain.
What are blossoms?
Rav Pappa: a thin cloud beneath a thick cloud.
Rav Yehuda: a mist before the rain comes, and rain after rain signals the rain is ending.
Other signs: the rain's end is marked by a particular kind of lightning and the blackening of goat-herds.
Ulla visited Babylonia, saw the blossoms, and told them to pack up since rain would not come; the Babylonians deceive about rain.
Ulla in Babylonia saw a full basket of dates sold cheaply and honey sold cheaply, and said the Babylonians do not engage in Torah study.
A baraita: Rabbi Eliezer says the whole world drinks from the waters of the ocean.
Genesis verse: a mist went up from the earth and watered the whole face of the ground.
Rabbi Yehoshua objects that the ocean waters are salty.
Rabbi Eliezer replies that they are sweetened by passing through clouds.
Rabbi Yehoshua says the whole world drinks from the waters above.
Deuteronomy verse: for the rain of heaven you drink water.
Rabbi Yehoshua reconciles the Genesis verse: clouds rise and receive rain water, like sieves.
Job verse: they draw up the drops of water, distilled into rain for its mist.
The clouds are perforated like a sieve and pour water onto the ground.
Samuel verse: He gathers waters in the thick clouds.
The distance between drop and drop is a hair's breadth, teaching that the day of rain is as great as the day heaven and earth were created.
Job verse: He does great things beyond searching.
Job verse: He gives rain upon the face of the earth.
Isaiah verse, and Psalm verse: He covers the mountains with His might.
According to whom does this go?
Psalm verse: He waters the mountains from His upper chambers.
Rabbi Yohanan: His upper chambers are the Holy One's, following Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer, since rain ascends there.
Otherwise the verse would not be read this way.
Deuteronomy verse: the Lord will make the rain of your land dust and powder from heaven.
How can this be found?
Since it descends from heaven, it is so called; here too, since it ascends there, the upper chambers are so called. By whose view does this go?
Rabbi Hanina said this.
Psalm verse: He gathers the waters of the sea as a heap and puts the depths in storehouses.
Who caused the storehouses of the depths to fill? Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua each hold that view.

10a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita: the Land of Israel was created first, and the rest of the world was created afterward.
Proverbs verse: before He had made the earth and the outskirts, cited for the order of creation.
The Holy One Himself waters the Land of Israel.
The whole world is watered through an agent.
Job verse: He gives rain upon the face of the earth and sends waters upon the fields, cited about the Land of Israel.
The Land of Israel drinks rainwater.
The whole world draws from it.
Job verse: He gives rain upon the face of the earth.
The Land of Israel drinks first.
The whole world drinks afterward.
Job verse: He gives rain upon the face of the earth.
A parable: one who kneads cheese first takes the edible part and sets aside the waste.
The Master said the clouds sweeten the water.
How do we know this? Rabbi Yohanan's source is asked for.
Psalm verse: He covered Himself with dark waters, thick clouds of the skies.
Samuel verse: He drew waters from thick clouds.
The two verses are reconciled by reading the word differently.
Rabbi Yehoshua holds a view based on these verses.
Rav Dimi reports that in the West they say small clouds are bright and large clouds are dark.
According to whom does this go?
A baraita: the upper waters hang by a word, and their fruit is rain.
Psalm verse: the earth is satisfied with the fruit of Your works.
This follows the view of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer.
The water comes from the work of the Holy One's own hands.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: the whole world draws from the Garden of Eden.
Genesis verse: a river went out of Eden to water the garden.
A tanna teaches a saying about the whole world drinking from a measure drawn from a house-kor.
A baraita on relative sizes: Egypt is a sixtieth of Kush, Kush a sixtieth of the world, the world a sixtieth of the Garden, and the Garden a sixtieth of Gehenna.
Other opinions: Gehenna and Eden each have no fixed measure.
Rabbi Oshaya asks what the Jeremiah verse means.
Jeremiah verse: O dweller upon many waters, rich in treasures.
Why does Babylon's treasury fill? Because she dwells upon many waters.
Rav: Babylonia is a dry land that has no rain and is rich in water.
Abaye: we hold, let me be drowned rather than dried.
Mishnah: on the sixteenth of Marheshvan one begins asking for rain; Rabban Gamliel says on the fifteenth day after the festival, so the last Israelite reaches the Euphrates.
Rabbi Elazar: the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel.
A baraita: Hananya says the Diaspora asks until the sixtieth day after the equinox.
Rav Huna bar Hiyya, citing Shmuel: the halakha follows Hananya.
Is that so? They asked Shmuel from when we mention the giving of dew and rain.
Shmuel told them: it is a single measure, from when people bring their boats to the shore.
They raised the question: sixty days before or sixty days after?
A baraita: Rav says sixty days after the equinox, and Shmuel says sixty days before it.
Rabbi Naḥman bar Yitzḥak gives a mnemonic, and Rav Pappa rules that the halakha is sixty days after the equinox.
Mishnah: if the seventeenth of Marheshvan passes without rain, individuals begin three fasts, and they may eat, drink, and bathe in the evening.
Mishnah: if the first of Kislev passes without rain, the court decrees three fasts on the community.
Who holds the view about individuals?
Rav Huna says it is the Rabbis.
Rav Huna: individuals fast three fasts on Monday, Thursday, and Monday.
What does this teach us?
We learned: the court does not decree a fast on the community at the beginning on Thursday, so as not to raise prices, but only the first three fasts on Monday, Thursday, and Monday.
Why teach this? It might be said that this applies only to the community, but not to individuals.
A baraita likewise: when individuals begin to fast, they fast on Monday, Thursday, and Monday, and they stop at the beginning of months.

10b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Sages taught about the festive days recorded in the Scroll of Fasting.
A baraita: a person should not say he is a student and not fit to be an individual.
Rather, all disciples of the Sages are individuals.
What is an individual, and who is a student who is an individual?
An individual is anyone fit to be appointed leader over the community.
A student is anyone who is asked a halakhic question and answers in his studies.
This applies even in a tractate like Kallah.
A baraita: not everyone who wishes to make himself an individual does so; a student does so, according to Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yose says: one does so and remembers it for good, since it is not praise for him but suffering.
Another baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view, are cited.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view is limited to matters of praise; in matters of suffering, one does so and remembers it for good.
A baraita: one who fasted for trouble that passed, or for a sick person who recovered, continues fasting and completes the fast.
One traveling from a place that does not fast to a place that does fasts with them.
One traveling from a place that fasts to a place that does not fast fasts and completes the fast.
If one forgot and ate or drank, he should not appear before the community and should not conduct himself with festivity.
Genesis verses: Jacob told his sons why they should not appear before Esau and Ishmael, lest they be envied.
Genesis verse: Joseph told his brothers, do not be agitated on the way.
Rabbi Elazar: Joseph told his brothers not to engage in halakha lest they be agitated on the way.
Objection: but Rabbi Elai bar Berekhiah said two Torah scholars walking on the road without words of Torah between them are fit to be burned.
Kings verse: as they went on, a chariot of fire and horses of fire appeared and separated them.
The reason: when there is speech between them they are not fit to burn; without speech, they are.
No contradiction: one is for study, the other for reflection on the baraita as taught.
A baraita: do not take a large stride, and bring the sun into the city; do not take a large stride.
The Master said that a large stride takes one five-hundredth of a person's eyesight.
Following Rav Yehuda, who said Rav: a person should leave and enter in good weather.
Genesis verse: at morning light, the men were sent away.
Rav Yehuda said Rabbi Hiyya: one walking on the road should not eat more than two hungers' worth.
What is the reason here? In the West they say it is due to sustenance, and asks what the difference is between the two reasons.

11a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gemara's alternative case distinguishing a traveler sitting in a boat from one moving between stations.
Rav Pappa ate a loaf each parasang, reasoning that the danger lay in digestion and he was healthy.
Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav: one who starves himself in famine years is spared an unusual death.
Job 5:20 is cited to support this, read closely for its wording.
Why does the verse say from death by famine rather than simply from famine?
Rather, the verse means that starving in famine earns a reward of being saved from an unusual death.
Reish Lakish: a man may not have relations with his wife during famine years.
Genesis 41:50 is cited, noting that Joseph's sons were born before the famine came.
A baraita permits childless men to have relations during famine, contradicting Reish Lakish.
Baraita: when the community suffers and one man separates himself, angels exclude him from its consolation.
A parallel baraita: one may not say he will go home to eat and drink while the community suffers.
Isaiah 22:13 is quoted as the example of feasting during public distress.
The continuation, Isaiah 22:14, shows that such a person's sin is not expiated.
The baraita concludes that this is the attribute of average people who merely exclude themselves from suffering.
The baraita turns to the attribute of wicked people and introduces a verse about them.
Isaiah 56:12 and 57:1 are cited to describe the wicked and the righteous taken early to spare them harm.
The baraita's conclusion: one should share the distress of the community, as Moses did.
Exodus 17:12 describes Moses sitting on a stone during the battle with Amalek.
Why did Moses have to sit on a rock rather than on a cushion?
Moses chose to share Israel's distress, so he sat in discomfort with them.
Anyone who shares the community's distress merits seeing its consolation.
A baraita warns against thinking one's secret deeds are unseen and names witnesses who will testify.
Habakkuk 2:11 is cited: stones and beams will speak out against a man.
In Rabbi Sheila's school: the two accompanying angels will testify against a person.
Psalms 91:11 is cited to show that angels are charged over a person.
Rabbi Hidka: a person's own soul will testify against him.
Micah 7:5 is cited to support the soul as a witness.
Others say a person's own limbs will testify against him.
Isaiah 43:10 is cited: you are My witnesses, says the Lord.
Deuteronomy 32:4 is cited to open the baraita's exegesis of divine justice.
Exegesis of faithfulness: the wicked are punished in the World-to-Come even for minor sins, and the righteous in this world.
Exegesis of without iniquity: the righteous are rewarded in the World-to-Come, and the wicked for minor mitzvot in this world.
The third part of the verse, he is just and righteous, is cited.
The Sages teach that at death a person's deeds are displayed to him and he must confirm them.
The deeds recite what he did, and he confirms it and signs an acknowledgment.
Job 37:7 is cited for the idea that each person signs his own deeds.
He even affirms the judgment as just and says that he was rightly judged.
Psalms 51:6 is cited for being justified when God judges.
Shmuel: whoever sits in a fast is called a sinner.
The Gemara identifies the tanna behind Shmuel's view: the baraita of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar.
What does the verse mean by atoning for sinning with the soul?
Numbers 6:11 is cited about the nazirite's atonement for sinning by the soul.
With what soul did this nazirite actually sin?
The nazirite sinned by afflicting himself through abstaining from wine.
A fortiori argument: if abstaining only from wine is sinful, abstaining from all food and drink is more so.
Rabbi Elazar: one who accepts a fast upon himself is called holy.
Numbers 6:5 is cited: the nazirite shall be holy and let his hair grow long.
A fortiori argument: if the nazirite who abstains from one thing is called holy, the faster is more so.
According to Shmuel, is the nazirite called holy, as Rabbi Elazar's verse states?
That verse refers to the sanctity of the growing locks, not to the nazirite himself.
According to Rabbi Elazar, is the nazirite called a sinner, as the verse seems to imply?
That verse refers to a nazirite who made himself impure by contact with the dead.
Did Rabbi Elazar really say that fasting is virtuous, given his teaching that one should always consider oneself?

11b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara reasons that a fasting person is like a sacred object housed inside him, which must not be harmed.
Hosea 11:9 is cited: the sacred one is in your midst.
The contradiction is resolved: the first ruling applies when one can fast without harm, the second when he cannot.
Reish Lakish: one who fasts is called pious.
Proverbs 11:17 is cited, reading gomel as weaning oneself from unnecessary pleasure.
Rav Sheshet: a student who fasts has let a dog eat his meal, since the fast leaves him too weak to study.
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba: there is no communal fast in Babylonia other than the Ninth of Av.
Reish Lakish, via Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba: a Torah scholar may not fast, because it saps his strength for Torah.
The mishna's rule: during the first fasts people eat and drink after dark and begin fasting in the morning.
Rav Huna, via Rabbi Zeira: one who accepted a fast and ate all night still recites the fast prayer the next day.
Rav Yosef asks what Rav Huna holds: do a few hours of fasting count as a fast at all, or only lack the prayer?
Abaye answers that Rav Huna holds hours do count, but the extra night hours were not accepted at the outset.
Mar Ukva visits Ginzak and is asked questions he cannot immediately answer.
First question: does one fast for hours, or does one not fast for hours?
Second question: are gentile wine jars permanently prohibited, or can they be made permitted?
Third question: in what garments did Moses serve during the seven days of inauguration?
Mar Ukva goes to the study hall to ask the questions.
The halakha: one fasts for hours and even recites the fast prayer.
The halakha: gentile jars are permitted once they have gone unused for twelve months.
Moses served in a special white cloak, neither his own clothes nor the regular priestly garments.
Rav Kahana taught that Moses's white cloak had no hem.
Rav Hisda begins a further statement, cut off at the end of the daf.

12a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The ruling that one may fast for a few hours, provided he took it on and tasted nothing until evening.
Abaye objects that this is obvious, since such a fast is a full fast that lasts the whole day.
Rav Hisda replies that the ruling is needed for one who changed his mind midday and fasted a few more hours.
Rav Hisda: any fast on which the sun does not set is not called a fast at all.
Objection: the priestly watch fasts on a communal fast but does not complete it, which implies a partial fast counts.
Reply: there they abstained only to cause themselves distress, out of solidarity, so it was not a real fast.
Another objection: Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok's family postponed the Ninth of Av fast and did not complete it.
Reply: they too merely caused themselves distress, so the case shows nothing about a real fast.
Objection from Rabbi Yohanan, who said he would fast until he returned home, implying a short fast.
Reply: he said this only to excuse himself from dining at the Nasi's house, so it was no real fast.
Shmuel: any fast not accepted upon oneself while it was still day is not called a fast.
If someone sat in fasting that day anyway, how is that considered?
Rabba bar Sheila: such a person is like a bellows full of air, which is not a fast.
When does one take a fast upon himself?
Rav: one accepts the fast in the afternoon of the preceding day, from midday onward.
Shmuel: one accepts the fast at the end of the afternoon prayer.
Rav Yosef: Shmuel's view is the sound one, as shown by the wording of Megillat Taanit.
Does the wording mean he binds himself at the time of prayer, as the plain reading suggests?
No: the word should be read as yei'aser, meaning he prohibits himself from fasting on those days.
Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi disagree about whether the text reads yeisar or yei'aser.
What is the source for the reading yei'aser, according to the one who holds that the text is prohibitive?
A baraita in Megillat Taanit: one who bound himself beforehand to fast on these days is prohibited from fasting.
An illustration: a private person who took on Monday and Thursday fasts all year, and the Festival days fell on them, is governed by which came first.
A baraita: until when may one eat and drink on communal fasts? Until dawn, per Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, or until the cock crows, per Rabbi Elazar.
Abaye: this applies only if one has not finished his meal, since one who finished may not eat more.
Rava objects with a baraita that permits eating after finishing a meal and rising.
Abaye replies that there the table was not yet cleared, so the meal was not finished.
Some report Rava's version: the ruling applies only if one did not sleep after eating.
Abaye objects with a baraita that permits eating after sleeping and rising during the night.
Rava replies that there the baraita refers to one who was merely dozing, not fully asleep.
What are the circumstances of dozing?
Rav Ashi begins to answer, and the daf ends mid-statement.

12b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ashi explains dozing: one is asleep yet not fully asleep, and he can recall what just happened when reminded.
Rav Kahana, citing Rav: an individual who accepted a fast may not wear shoes that day, lest he had accepted a communal fast.
How should one act to avoid this problem?
Rabba bar Rav Sheila: one should recite the formula that he is before God in an individual fast tomorrow.
The Sages objected to Rav Sheshet: they saw scholars wearing shoes and going to the study house on a communal fast.
Rav Sheshet grew angry and replied that perhaps those scholars also ate, if they treated the fast lightly.
Abaye and Rava entered the synagogue wearing their shoes upside down, and Mareimar and Mar Zutra swapped their shoes.
These practices follow Shmuel's ruling that in Babylonia the only stringent communal fast is the Ninth of Av.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: one may borrow his fast and repay it on another day.
Shmuel objected: a fast is only a self-affliction, so one must repay it only if able to afflict himself.
Another version: Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, says one may borrow a fast and repay it.
Shmuel replied that this is obvious and that it should be considered a vow.
Shmuel's logic: a vow must be repaid at some point, so the fast must be repaid on a later day.
Rav Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi, visited the house of Rav Asi, who prepared a calf for him.
They asked him to taste something from the meal.
He replied that he was sitting in an observed fast and could not eat.
They objected that he should borrow and repay the fast, as Rav Yehuda cited Rav's rule.
He replied that it was a fast for a dream, undertaken to counteract a bad dream.
Rav's teaching that a fast neutralizes a bad dream, as fire burns chaff, and how this applies.
Rav Hisda: the fast is effective only on the very day the dream was had.
Rav Yosef: one suffering from a bad dream may fast even on Shabbat.
What is the remedy for one who has fasted on Shabbat, denigrating it?
He should observe another fast on another day to atone for the Shabbat fast.
Mishna: if the first three fasts passed without rain, the court decrees three further, severe fasts on the community.
On these severe fasts one may eat and drink only before nightfall and may not work, bathe, anoint, wear shoes, or cohabit.
If these also passed without an answer, the court decrees seven more, for thirteen fasts in all.
On these seven fasts they sound the alarm and lock the shops, though shops open on Monday evening and on Thursday for Shabbat.
If still unanswered, the community adopts mourning customs and reduces business, building, betrothals, and greetings.
Individual Torah scholars fast each Monday and Thursday until Nisan ends, after which rain is a sign of curse.
First Samuel 12:17 is cited: is not the wheat harvest today, and I will call for thunder and rain.
Granted that the other prohibitions give pleasure, why must one refrain from work, which is suffering?
Rav Hisda, citing Rav Yirmeya bar Abba: the fast day is linked to the Joel verse, which teaches the derivation.
Joel 1:14 is cited: sanctify a fast, call a solemn assembly, gather the elders.
Just as a solemn assembly forbids work, so too a fast forbids work.
If so, should the prohibition on work begin from the evening, as with an assembly?
Rabbi Zeira: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba explained that the verse compares the fast to a gathering of elders, which occurs by day.
Could one instead say the fast begins at a different time, taking the day's purification into account?
Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi supports Rav Huna, who said the public gathering occurs in the morning hours.
How do they conduct the communal gathering on a fast day?
Abaye: from morning until midday they examine the affairs of the town and correct its deficiencies.
From then until a quarter of the day they read a portion of the Torah and a haftara.
From then on they pray and petition for mercy.
Nehemiah 9:3 is cited: they stood and read from the Torah for a quarter of the day, and confessed for another quarter.

13a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Could one reverse the order, praying first and then attending to the community's concerns?
It should not enter your mind to say so, since the order of events is fixed.
Ezra 9:4 and 9:5 are cited to show that communal matters come before personal prayer.
Rafram bar Pappa, citing Rav Hisda: bathing forbidden for mourning applies to hot and cold water, while bathing for pleasure is forbidden only in hot water.
Rav Idi bar Avin: the mishna's phrase they lock the bathhouses shows that only hot-water bathing is forbidden.
Abaye objects: if cold bathing were also forbidden, the mishna should have said they dam the rivers.
Rav Sheisha, son of Rav Idi, asks what the mishna's clause adds, since bathing is already forbidden.
Conclusion: bathing is forbidden in hot water and permitted in cold water.
A baraita is proposed in support: all obligated in immersion immerse as usual on the Ninth of Av and Yom Kippur.
In what do they immerse, since hot water is drawn water and cannot be used for ritual immersion?
Rather, the baraita refers to cold water, permitting those obligated in immersion but not others.
Rav Hana bar Ketina: this is no proof, since the baraita addresses only the warm springs of Tiberias.
Objection: the mishna's closing clause says the Deputy High Priest loses his immersion, so cold water should have been permitted.
Rav Pappa: the baraita refers to a place where cold water is unavailable, only hot springs.
A baraita: the work prohibition applies only by day, the shoe prohibition only in town, and the bathing prohibition only to the whole body.
The baraita continues: shoes are allowed on the road and removed upon entering town.
Bathing the face, hands, and feet is permitted, and the same applies to an ostracized person and a mourner.
Objection: if the baraita means hot water, washing face hands and feet would be forbidden, per Rav Sheshet's ruling on fingers.
Reply: the baraita means hot water, and the similar clause refers to work and shoes, not bathing.
Rabbi Abba the priest, citing Rabbi Yosei the priest: Rabbi Yosei bathed in cold water through seven days of mourning.
Reply: his mourning periods came in quick succession, and a baraita permits lightening the hair and washing garments then.
Rav Hisda clarifies the baraita: one may trim with a razor, not scissors, and wash garments in water, not natron or sand.
Rava: a mourner may bathe in cold water all seven days, just as he may eat meat and drink wine.
The Gemara raises an objection.

13b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita: a grown woman may not render herself unattractive during mourning for her father, unlike a young girl.
Does the baraita concern bathing, and if so, in what water may a grown woman bathe?
Objection from Rav Hisda's ruling that a mourner may not insert even a finger into hot water for washing.
No, the baraita is not about bathing; it concerns painting the eyes and dyeing the hair.
The earlier baraita about Rabbi Yosei's sons is proposed as support for Rava's ruling.
This is no proof: Rabbi Yosei's mourning periods came in succession, which permits lightening the hair and washing garments.
Rav Hisda's ruling on washing garments, with the restrictions on razors, scissors, natron, sand, and iceplant.
Another version: Rava held that a mourner may not bathe in cold water for all seven days.
What is the difference from meat and wine, which a mourner may consume?
Meat and wine are there to relieve his anxieties, so he may fortify himself with them.
The baraita on a grown woman's unattractiveness is proposed as support for Rava's ruling.
In what water may a grown woman bathe, if the baraita concerns bathing at all?
Objection from Rav Hisda again: a mourner may not insert even a finger into hot water.
No, the baraita speaks of painting the eyes and dyeing the hair, not of bathing.
Rav Hisda: the same reasoning applies to laundry, so a mourner may not wash laundry during the seven days.
The practical halakha: a mourner may not bathe his body in either hot or cold water, but his face, hands, and feet may be washed in cold water.
Smearing with oil is forbidden even in small amounts, but removing dirt is permitted.
How does one mention the fast prayer in the Amida?
Rav Yehuda permitted his son Rav Yitzhak to expound publicly, and Rav Yitzhak taught that an individual fasting recites the fast prayer.
Where in the Amida is this recited?
Rav Yitzhak objects: may an individual establish a blessing for himself beyond the fixed blessings?
Rav Yitzhak clarifies: one mentions the fast in the blessing of Who listens to prayer, as Rav Sheshet also said.
Objection from a baraita: an individual prays eighteen blessings and the community nineteen.
What is meant by an individual and a community in this context?
If community means the prayer leader, the communal fast Amida has twenty-four blessings, not nineteen.
Reinterpretation: the baraita compares an individual on an individual fast with one on a communal fast, so an individual may add a personal blessing.
Reply: the community refers to the prayer leader, and the first three fasts have only eighteen plus one blessing.
Are the six additional blessings not recited on the first series of communal fasts?
A baraita: the difference between the first three and the middle three fasts is only permitted or forbidden work, so all else is identical.
The tanna taught some differences and omitted others, so the baraita's list is not exhaustive.
But the baraita says the difference is only, which means it lists every difference.
Rather, the tanna speaks of the prohibitions of fast days, not of details of prayer.
Alternatively, the middle three fasts also do not include all twenty-four blessings, since they are recited only on the last series.
Objection: the baraita on the middle and last seven fasts says the difference is only alarm and locked stores, so all else is identical.
If one says the tanna omitted here too, the phrase the difference is only would be meaningless.
Does the phrase the difference is only indeed mean there is only a single difference?

14a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: But the tanna omitted the ark, which was carried through the streets on the last seven fast days.
Reply: if the omission concerns the ark, it is not a real omission, since the tanna teaches only private matters, not public ones.
Rav Ashi: the mishna's wording is precise, since it says these days are more stringent only in alarm and locked stores.
Objection: here too the tanna may have omitted something, yet the mishna's phrasing indicates a single difference.
How can one read the phrasing as indicating a single difference, given that the ark was omitted?
The omission is not real: the tanna treats the ark in another chapter, where it is mentioned.
The matter of the twenty-four blessings is likewise not an omission, since it is taught in another chapter.
What halakhic conclusion was reached about where the Aneinu prayer is inserted?
Rav, via Shmuel bar Sasretai and Rav Hiyya bar Ashi: insert it between the blessings of Who redeems and Who heals.
Rav Ashi, citing Rabbi Yannai: insert it in the blessing of Who listens to prayer, which is the halakha.
Baraita one: pregnant and nursing women fast on the first fasts but not the last ones.
Baraita two: pregnant and nursing women fast on the last fasts but not the first ones.
Baraita three: pregnant and nursing women do not fast on either set.
Rav Ashi: take the middle fasts as decisive, which reconciles all three baraitot.
The mishna: these seven fasts are more stringent only in sounding the alarm and locking the stores.
With what do they sound the alarm?
Rav Yehuda says with shofarot, while Rav Yehuda bar Shmuel bar Sheilat, citing Rav, says with the Aneinu prayer.
It might be that each of these Sages denied the other's form of alarm, since only one can be the valid one.
But a baraita says the court decrees at least seven fasts with eighteen alarms, and Jericho's shofar episodes refute the Aneinu view.
Rather, both sides agree shofarot are called alarm, and they differ only over whether Aneinu is called alarm.
If so, one who holds Aneinu is alarm also holds shofarot, while one who holds shofarot does not allow Aneinu.
A baraita: for other calamities such as locusts or snakes they cry out rather than sound the alarm, so alarm is with shofarot.
This is a dispute between tanna'im, as the mishna on sounding alarm on Shabbat shows, with Rabbi Yosei's view.
If the alarm is with shofarot, is sounding them permitted on Shabbat?
Rather, it refers to Aneinu, which the mishna calls sounding the alarm, so some tanna holds that alarm is by prayer.
In the years of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, the community suffered a trouble.

14b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia decreed thirteen fasts without being answered, and considered decreeing more.
Rabbi Ami objects that the community should not be burdened beyond measure, so no more than thirteen fasts.
Rabbi Abba: Rabbi Ami ruled on his own authority, against the majority opinion.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba, citing Rabbi Yohanan: the thirteen-fast limit applies only to rain, while other calamities continue until answered.
A baraita states the same: the three and seven fasts apply only to rain, and other calamities are fasted until answered.
Let this baraita refute Rabbi Ami's view.
Rabbi Ami could say it is a dispute between tanna'im, with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi against Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Baraita: no more than thirteen fasts, since the community is not burdened excessively, per Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
The people of Nineveh ask Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi how to pray for drought in the summer: as individuals or as a community?
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi replies they are like individuals and pray for rain in the blessing of Who listens to prayer.
A baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says the rain prayer is in the blessing of the years only when the land is inhabited as it should be.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi is himself a tanna, so he may dispute the baraita's opinion.
What halakhic conclusion was reached on this matter?
Rav Nahman says one prays in the blessing of the years, while Rav Sheshet says in Who listens to prayer.
The halakha: when rain is needed out of season in Eretz Yisrael, one prays in the blessing of Who listens to prayer.
Mishna: on Monday shops open a little at nightfall, and on Thursday all day in deference to Shabbat.
Does the mishna mean shops open only a little on both days, or a little on Monday and fully on Thursday?
A baraita resolves the dilemma: on Monday they open a little until evening, and on Thursday all day.
Shops with two entrances open one and lock the other, and a shop with a platform hiding its door may open normally.
Mishna: if these fasts also pass unanswered, they decrease business, building, and planting.
Tosefta: building and planting refer only to joyful building, such as a wedding chamber for a son.
Joyful planting refers to a splendid royal garden planted purely for ornamentation.
The mishna also says they decrease greetings between people.
The Sages: ḥaverim do not greet each other, and ordinary people who greet them are answered in a subdued, solemn manner.
Rabbi Elazar: an important person may fall on his face only if he is certain of being answered.
Joshua son of Nun is cited, to whom God said: why are you fallen upon your face?
Rabbi Elazar: an important person may wear sackcloth in prayer only if he is certain of being answered.
Jehoram son of Ahab rent his clothes and wore sackcloth, and was answered despite his wickedness.
Rabbi Elazar: not all are worthy to petition by rending garments or by falling on the face.
Moses and Aaron fell on their faces, while Joshua and Caleb rent their garments, as Numbers 14 shows.
Rabbi Zeira objects: the word and in the verse suggests Joshua and Caleb did both, not one or the other.
Rabbi Elazar: in the messianic age kings serve God by rising and ministers by bowing.
Isaiah 49:7 is cited: kings shall see and rise, princes shall bow down.

15a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Isaiah 49:7 is quoted: kings shall see and arise, and princes shall bow down.
Rabbi Zeira objects, or some say Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani: if the verse said only ministers bow, the explanation would stand, but the and suggests both.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak: not all are fit for light and not all are fit for gladness.
The righteous are fit for light, and the upright are fit for gladness.
Psalms 97:11 is cited: light is sown for the righteous and gladness for the upright in heart.
The chapter closes, and the mishna asks what the customary order of fast days is.
Mishna: the ark is taken out to the city square, and ashes are placed on it and on the heads of the Nasi, the head of the court, and everyone.
The eldest of the community reproves the congregation, saying the Ninevites' deeds, not their sackcloth, are what God saw.
Jonah 3:10 and Joel 2:13 are cited to show that repentance in practice must accompany prayer and fasting.
They stand for prayer: an elder experienced in leading prayer, with children and a poor house, descends as prayer leader.
He recites twenty-four blessings: the eighteen daily blessings plus six, including Remembrances and Shofarot.
Psalms verses that open the additional blessings are cited: Psalms 120, 121, 130, and 102.
Rabbi Yehuda: the leader need not recite Remembrances and Shofarot, but instead recites the passage on famine and pestilence.
I Kings 8:37 and Jeremiah 14:1 are cited as the passages on famine and drought.
Concluding formula for the first blessing: He Who answered Abraham on Mount Moriah will answer you.
Concluding formula for the second blessing: He Who answered our forefathers at the Red Sea.
Concluding formula for the third blessing: He Who answered Joshua at Gilgal, with the shofar sounded at Jericho.
Concluding formula for the fourth blessing: He Who answered Samuel at Mizpah.
Concluding formula for the fifth blessing: He Who answered Elijah on Mount Carmel.
Concluding formula for the sixth blessing: He Who answered Jonah from the fish.
Concluding formula for the seventh blessing: He Who answered David and Solomon in Jerusalem, Who has mercy on the Land.
The mishna relates an incident, and the daf ends mid-sentence.

15b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: In the days of Rabbi Halafta and Rabbi Hananya ben Teradyon, a prayer leader finished the fast blessing without amen, and the attendant called for shofar blasts with each verse.
When the Sages heard this custom, they limited it to the Eastern Gate and Temple Mount, since it is not performed elsewhere.
Mishna, Rabbi Yehoshua: on the first three fasts the priestly watch fasts without completing, and the patrilineal family does not fast; the other sets differ accordingly.
The Sages disagree: on the first three fasts neither group fasts, and the later sets are divided differently.
Another difference: the priestly watch may drink wine at night but not by day, while the patrilineal family may not drink at all.
On days recorded in Megillat Taanit as forbidden for eulogy, eulogizing the day before is forbidden, but the day after is permitted.
Rabbi Yosei disagrees with the eulogy restrictions, and also with the fasting restrictions on the day before and after.
One may not decree a communal fast beginning on a Thursday, so as not to raise prices before Shabbat.
Rabbi Yosei: just as the first three fasts do not begin on Thursday, neither do the later series; all begin on a Monday.
No communal fast is decreed on New Moons, Hanukkah, or Purim, and if begun, the sequence is not interrupted, per Rabban Gamliel.
Rabbi Meir: even Rabban Gamliel concedes that on these days the fast is not completed.
Likewise, when the Ninth of Av falls on Shabbat eve, one eats before Shabbat and does not complete the fast.
Gemara citing the mishna: the order of fast days begins with removing the ark.
Is this performed even on the first set of fasts?
A baraita contradicts: on the first two sets everyone enters the synagogue and prays the usual prayers, with no ark removal.
The baraita continues: on the final seven fasts the ark is removed to the city square and ashes are placed on it and on heads.
Rabbi Natan: they bring specifically burnt ashes.
Rav Pappa: the mishna too taught the full ritual only for the final seven fasts.
The mishna: ashes are placed on the Nasi and deputy Nasi, and then each member of the community places ashes on his head.
Is this the proper order, given a baraita on matters of greatness and curses?
Leviticus 10:6 and 10:7 show Moses addressing Aaron first in matters of honor, and the curse of the serpent, Eve, and Adam began with the least.
The leaders perform the expressions of mourning as a distinction, since the community entrusts them with requesting compassion for all.
Rav Ada: each person places ashes on his own head.
Each member of the community places ashes on his own head, including the Nasi and head of the court.
Why should the Nasi and head of the court not take their own ashes?
What is different that someone else takes the ashes and places them on their heads?
Rabbi Abba of Caesarea: it is intentional, since one who humiliates himself is not like one humiliated by others.

ranges.en: The ashes are placed on the leaders' heads by others, so that their suffering is more visible and they are humbled.
Where exactly are the ashes placed on the head?
Rabbi Yitzhak: on the place of the tefillin, as Isaiah 61:3 likens ashes on the head to an ornament.
A mnemonic for the coming statements: the square, the ark, sackcloth, ashes, cemetery, and Moriah.
Why do they go out to the square?
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba: a symbolic act, saying that private crying went unanswered, so they now publicly disgrace themselves.
Reish Lakish: going out to the square symbolizes exile, and may our exile atone for us.
What is the practical difference between these two explanations?
The difference: if they moved from one synagogue to another, Reish Lakish's exile suffices, while Rabbi Hiyya's private-to-public view does not.
Why do they remove the ark to the city square?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: a modest vessel that was always hidden is now exposed due to our transgressions.
Why do they cover themselves in sackcloth?
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba: we are considered like animals before You, which are covered with hides.
Why do they place burnt ashes on the ark?
Rabbi Yehuda ben Pazi: God says, I am with him in trouble, quoting Psalms 91:15.
Reish Lakish: the same idea is derived from Isaiah 63:9, in all their affliction He was afflicted.
Rabbi Zeira recounts his reaction when he first saw the Sages place burnt ashes on the ark: his whole body trembled.
Why do they place ashes on the head of each individual?
Rabbi Levi bar Hama and Rabbi Hanina disagree on this matter.
One says: we are considered like ashes before You.
The other says: the ashes remind God of the ashes of Isaac our forefather, on our behalf.
What is the practical difference between the two explanations?
The difference is ordinary earth, which symbolizes self-nullification but lacks any connection to Isaac.
Why do they go out to the cemetery on a fast day?
Rabbi Levi bar Hama and Rabbi Hanina disagree again: one says we are like the dead before You.
The other says the cemetery visit is so the deceased will request mercy on our behalf.
What is the practical difference between these two explanations?
The difference concerns graves of gentiles, which suffice only for the first explanation.
What is the meaning of the name Mount Moriah, as Chronicles 3:1 mentions, and what do they dispute?
Rabbi Levi bar Hama: the name refers to the Great Sanhedrin, from which instruction went out to Israel.
Rabbi Hanina: the name refers to the fear that went out from the mountain to the nations of the world.
Mishna: the eldest of the community says statements of reproof to the congregation.
Baraita: if there is an elder, he gives the reproof, and if not, a scholar, and if not, a person of imposing appearance.
Is an elder preferred to a scholar simply because of age, even if he is not a scholar?
Abaye: an elder who is also a scholar gives the reproof, and if no scholar is available, even a young scholar does.
Reproof content: it is not sackcloth and fasting that atone, but repentance and good deeds, as at Nineveh.
Jonah 3:10 is cited: God saw their deeds, that they turned from their evil way.
Jonah 3:8 is cited: man and beast shall be covered with sackcloth.
What did the people of Nineveh actually do?
They separated the animals and their young, and said they would not show mercy to animals if God showed none to them.
Jonah 3:8 is cited: and let them cry mightily to God.
What did they say that is described as crying out mightily?
They argued that the righteous should yield to the wicked, as the submissive yields to the intractable, so God should have mercy.
Jonah 3:8 is cited: each must turn from his evil way and from the violence in his hands.
What is the meaning of and from the violence that is in their hands?
Shmuel: the king of Nineveh ordered that even a stolen beam be removed from a building and returned to its owner.
Rav Adda bar Ahava: one who confesses a sin without repenting is like one holding a dead creeping animal in his hand.
To what is such a person comparable?
Immersion is ineffective while the source of impurity remains in the hand, but effective once the animal is thrown away.
Proverbs 28:13 and Lamentations 3:41 are cited: confession must be accompanied by forsaking sin and raising the heart.
Mishna: they stood for prayer, and the congregation appoints an elder to descend before the ark.
Baraita: even if an elder scholar is present, one appoints only a person accustomed to lead prayer.
Who is considered an accustomed prayer leader?
Rabbi Yehuda: one with dependent children who must toil in the field and whose house is empty, so he prays with devotion.
Rabbi Yehuda continues: he must be humble, have a pleasant voice, know Scripture and Mishna, and know all the blessings.
The Sages turned their eyes toward Rav Yitzhak bar Ami, who possessed all these qualities.

ranges.en: If one with dependent children and no means is the same as one whose house is empty, why does Rabbi Yehuda list both?
Rav Hisda: an empty house means empty of transgression.
Abaye: youthful bearing means one who had no bad reputation in his youth.
Jeremiah 12:8 is cited: my heritage has become to me as a lion in the forest, she has uttered her voice against me.
What is the meaning of she has uttered her voice against me?
Rabbi Elazar: this refers to an unworthy prayer leader, whose voice God finds hateful.
Mishna: the prayer leader recites twenty-four blessings, the eighteen daily ones plus six more.
Are these six, when in fact there are seven, as the mishna lists the seventh with Who has mercy on the Land?
Mishna: for the seventh blessing he recites Who has mercy on the Land.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak: the seventh counts only for length, since it is an extended sixth blessing.
Baraita: in Redeemer of Israel the leader lengthens the blessing and concludes with the Abraham formula, and the community answers amen.
Baraita: the second blessing concludes with the Red Sea formula, and the sexton calls for blasts after each blessing.
The sexton says blow for one blessing and blast for another, with this procedure for each additional blessing.
In what case is this said, and from where is it derived that one does not answer amen in the Temple?
Nehemiah 9:5 is cited: bless the Lord and let them say Blessed be Your glorious name, exalted above all blessing and praise.
The verse's repeated wording teaches that each blessing receives its own praise, so none is answered by amen in the Temple.
In the Temple the leader concludes the blessing with Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, and the congregation answers with a glorious kingdom formula.
In the Temple the sexton's blasts follow the formula for each blessing, until all the blessings are concluded.
Rabbi Halafta in Tzippori and Rabbi Hananya ben Teradyon in Sikhni established this custom, which the Sages limited to the Temple's eastern gate and mount.
Some say the baraita places the six additional blessings between Redeemer and Healer, and amen is answered for each blessing outside the Temple.
In the Temple they recite the formula without the congregation answering amen.
Why is there no amen in the Temple, and from where is that derived?
Nehemiah 9:5 is cited again as the source that no amen is answered in the Temple.
Sages' baraita: for the first blessing the leader recites the formula and the Abraham verse, with blasts and answers.
For the second blessing the leader recites the formula, and the congregation answers with the glorious kingdom formula.
The sexton calls for blasts as the leader recites the Red Sea verse, with blasts for each blessing in turn.
The blasts follow the procedure for each blessing until all are concluded.
Halafta and Hananya's custom was limited by the Sages to the Eastern Gate and Temple Mount.
Mishna: Rabbi Yehuda says the prayer leader did not need the Remembrances and Shofarot passages.
Rabbi Adda of Jaffa asks Rabbi Yehuda's reason, since Remembrances and Shofarot are not recited.

ranges.en: The mishna: the shofar is sounded on Rosh HaShana, on Jubilee Yom Kippur, and in war, and for the first blessing one recites He Who answered Abraham.
A baraita: some reverse the conclusions, saying Who hears cries for Elijah's blessing and Who hears prayer for Samuel's.
Granted for Samuel, where both prayer and crying are written, but for Elijah, where only prayer is written, how is crying the conclusion?
Elijah's words, Answer me, Lord, answer me, are an expression of crying, even without the word itself.
Mishna: for the sixth blessing he recites He Who answered Jonah, and for the seventh He Who answered David.
Since Jonah came after David and Solomon, why is Jonah mentioned first?
So that the series ends with Who has mercy on the Land; the Sumakhos tradition says the final blessing is Who humbles the exalted.
The mishna: on the first three fasts the priestly watch fasts but does not complete the fast.
Sages taught: why are priestly watch members permitted to drink wine at night but not by day?
Lest the Temple service become burdensome and they be called to assist the patrilineal family, so they must not drink by day.
Why may the patrilineal family not drink wine at all, day or night?
Because they are constantly engaged in the Temple service.
Even now, a priest who knows his watch and his family's watch is forbidden wine for that entire day, in case the Temple is rebuilt.
A priest who knows his watch but not his family's day is forbidden wine for that entire week.
A priest who knows neither is forbidden wine for the entire year.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: any priest is forbidden wine at any time, but the decree cannot be sustained after so many years.
Abaye: priests drink nowadays in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Mishna: priests in watch and standing may not cut hair or launder during the week, but may on Thursday in deference to Shabbat.
What is the reason for these prohibitions?
Rabbah bar bar Hana, citing Rabbi Yohanan: so that priests groom before entering their watch unkempt.
Baraita: a king cuts his hair daily, the High Priest on Friday before Shabbat, and an ordinary priest once every thirty days.
What is the reason a king cuts his hair daily?
Rabbi Abba bar Zavda: a king must always look his best, as the verse about the king in his beauty indicates.
Isaiah 33:17 is cited: your eyes shall see the king in his beauty.
The High Priest cuts his hair every Friday, since the watches change then.
What is the reason the High Priest cuts his hair every Friday?
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzhak: the watches are renewed every Friday, so each watch should see the High Priest well groomed.
An ordinary priest cuts his hair once every thirty days.
From where is the number thirty derived?
Verbal analogy: pera in Ezekiel 44:20 for priests matches pera in Numbers 6:5 for the nazirite, whose period is thirty days.
How do we know that a nazirite himself may not cut his hair for thirty days?
Rav Mattana: an unspecified naziriteship lasts thirty days, derived from the numerical value of yihye in Numbers 6:5.
Rav Pappa objects to Abaye: perhaps the verse means they should not let hair grow at all, cutting it daily.
Abaye replies: had the verse said they shall not let locks grow, that would be so, but since it says not suffer locks to grow long, they may have locks.
If cutting hair is required by Torah law, should even priests today cut their hair every thirty days?
The issue is like wine: as with one who drank wine, the prohibition applies when entering the Temple, not otherwise.
A baraita: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says priests are forbidden wine at all times, which contradicts Abaye's claim that priests drink like him.
