ranges.en: The prohibition is in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and one may infer that the Rabbis forbid wine for priests even now.
The reason is the hope for speedy rebuilding: a priest imbibing wine would delay Temple service, whereas cutting hair takes little time.
If so, a priest who drank wine could also sleep briefly and then enter, as Rami bar Abba's rule suggests.
Rami bar Abba: walking a mil or sleeping even a little dispels the effect of wine.
The Gemara rejects this: Rav Nahman, citing Rabba bar Avuh, limited the rule to a quarter-log, while more wine is not dispelled by such measures.
Rav Ashi: the Sages decreed against priests drinking wine, which desecrates service, but not against long hair, which does not.
A baraita lists those punished by Heaven, including priests who serve with wine or with long hair.
Wine is explicitly prohibited, but from where is the death penalty for long hair derived?
Ezekiel 44:20-21 juxtaposes the ban on long hair with the ban on wine, teaching that both carry the death penalty.
Inference: if juxtaposition makes wine and long hair alike, then long hair too desecrates service like wine.
No: the juxtaposition is only regarding death, not desecration of the service, so Rav Ashi's distinction holds.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi: before Ezekiel, who said this halakha, since prophets cannot innovate law?
Rav Ashi: by your logic the same problem arises for uncircumcised priests, which Rav Hisda learned from tradition and Ezekiel 44:9 supports.
Before Ezekiel, who taught that the uncircumcised may not serve?
Rather, it is learned as a definite tradition, and Ezekiel only supported it with a verse, so too for long hair.
Mishna: a day on which the Megillat Taanit forbids eulogy also forbids eulogizing the day before, but not the day after.
Baraita from Megillat Taanit: the days of fasting prohibition, and the days of eulogy prohibition, from the New Moon of Nisan through the festival.
The Gemara cites the baraita: from the New Moon of Nisan until the eighth, the daily offering was established, so no eulogy.
Why mention the New Moon at all? It could say from the second of Nisan, as the New Moon is already a holiday.
Rav: the New Moon is mentioned only to forbid eulogy on the day before, as the Megillat Taanit forbids fasting before such days.
Likewise, the day before the New Moon should be forbidden on its own, since fasting on the New Moon is forbidden.
The New Moon is by Torah law, which needs no reinforcement, so fasting the day before is permitted.
Baraita: days in Megillat Taanit are forbidden with the days before and after, unlike Shabbat and festivals, since rabbinic law needs reinforcement.
The Gemara cites the earlier ruling: from the eighth of Nisan to the end of Passover, eulogy is forbidden.
Why mention until the end of the festival? It could say until the festival, which is already forbidden.
Rav Pappa: this is explained like Rav's point: the first of Nisan must be mentioned to forbid the day before.

ranges.en: The Passover mention is needed only to prohibit eulogy on the day after, as the Megillat Taanit lists days.
In accordance with whose opinion is this ruling?
Rabbi Yosei, who prohibits eulogy both the day before and the day after the listed dates.
If so, why state the twenty-ninth of Adar as the day before the offering was established, rather than the day after the twenty-eighth?
Baraita from Megillat Taanit: on the twenty-eighth of Adar good tidings came, and the Jews were no longer restricted from Torah study, circumcision, and Shabbat.
Yehuda ben Shammua consulted a Roman matron, who advised them to cry out at night; they cried out and the decrees were annulled.
Abaye: the reason for the prohibition on the twenty-ninth of Adar is the case of a thirty-day Adar, which makes the day before the New Moon.
Rav Ashi: even if Adar has twenty-nine days, the twenty-ninth lies between two commemorative days and is itself treated as one.
The Master said in Megillat Taanit: from the eighth of Nisan until the end of Passover, eulogy is forbidden.
Why mention the eighth of Nisan, rather than the ninth, since the eighth is already prohibited as the day the offering was established?
If a calamity canceled the seven days of the offering, the eighth would remain forbidden as the first day Shavuot was restored.
The same logic applies to the twenty-ninth of Adar, which stays forbidden even if the twenty-eighth were canceled.
Rav Hiyya bar Asi, citing Rav: the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei, prohibiting eulogy on both the day before and the day after; Shmuel holds Rabbi Meir's view.
Did Shmuel really say this, since a baraita attributes the permission to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel?
Baraita: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel derives from the repeated on them that the day itself is forbidden while the days before and after are permitted.
Shmuel ruled that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Shmuel initially followed Rabbi Meir, since no other tanna was as lenient, but later adopted Rabban Shimon's more lenient view.
Bali reports that Rabbi Yohanan ruled in accordance with Rabbi Yosei.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba explains that Rabbi Yohanan spoke only of fasting before the dates, not of eulogy after them.
Did Rabbi Yohanan really say this, given his principle that the halakha follows an unattributed mishna, which permits reading earlier but not later?

ranges.en: Although the Sages decreed that certain places read the Scroll of Esther early, eulogy and fasting are permitted on those days.
When does this apply, and does it permit fasting and eulogy on the fourteenth in walled cities?
Megillat Taanit states that the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar are Purim days on which eulogy is forbidden.
Rava: the Megillat Taanit entry is needed only to forbid each group from fasting and eulogizing on the day on which it reads.
The difficulty continues: if the mishna refers to reading on the thirteenth, that day is Nicanor's Day, which is already a commemorative day.
Rather, the mishna refers to reading on the eleventh, which is the day before Trajan's Day, and it still permits fasting.
The mishna refers to those who read on the twelfth, and Trajan's Day itself was annulled, since Shemaya and Ahiya were killed that day.
Rav Nahman's fast on the twelfth was challenged, and he replied that Trajan's Day had been annulled by that event.
Why not derive that fasting on the twelfth is forbidden as the day before Nicanor's Day?
Rav Ashi: since Trajan's Day itself was annulled, one would not decree a fast on the twelfth for the sake of the next day, Nicanor's Day.
What is the origin of Nicanor's Day and of Trajan's Day?
A baraita: Nicanor, a Greek general, vowed to trample Jerusalem, and the Hasmoneans killed him and hung his thumbs and toes on the gates, on the thirteenth of Adar.
What is the origin of Trajan's Day?
Trajan sought to kill the leaders Luleyanus and Pappas, who answered that Nebuchadnezzar was a righteous king and Trajan a commoner unfit for miracles.
Luleyanus and Pappas argue that Trajan is a commoner, not a real king, so a miracle should not be performed through him.
They add that the Omnipresent placed them in Trajan's hands only so their blood would be avenged in the future.
Trajan killed them regardless, and two officials from Rome then clubbed him, establishing the day as a commemoration.
Mishna: one may not decree a communal fast starting on Thursday, or on New Moons, Hanukkah, or Purim, and an ongoing sequence is not interrupted.
How many fasts count as a beginning that cannot be interrupted?
Rav Aha: three fasts before the festival; Rabbi Asi: even one fast.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: the mishna's rule is Rabbi Meir's, in the name of Rabban Gamliel.
The Rabbis say a communal fast that falls on such a day is fasted and completed until nightfall, which is the practical halakha.
The chapter closes, and the mishna on the order of fasts applies when the first rain has not fallen.
Mishna: if vegetation was damaged by disease, or rain ceased for forty days, they cry out immediately.
Mishna: partial rain for vegetation but not trees, or for both but not cisterns, is cause for an immediate outcry.
Likewise, if one city received no rain while the surrounding area did, this is considered a divine curse.
Amos 4:7 is cited: I caused it to rain on one city and not another, and the portion not rained on withered.

ranges.en: Mishnah rules a city fasts and blows the shofar, while Rabbi Akiva reverses the two for pestilence and collapsing buildings
Asks what counts as a plague of pestilence that requires fasting and crying out
Five hundred able-bodied men and three deaths on consecutive days make a plague; fewer deaths do not
Blight, mildew, locusts, caterpillars, dangerous beasts and the sword call for crying out everywhere, since they spread
Elders decreed a land-wide fast over a little blight in Ashkelon and wolves seen in Transjordan; Rabbi Yosei says only sightings mattered
Crying out is allowed on Shabbat for siege, flood or a ship at sea; Rabbi Yosei and Shimon the Timnite differ, and the Sages reject Shimon
General rule: cry out for any community trouble except excess rain, and the story of Honi whose prayer for rain failed
Asks what Honi did after his prayer for rain went unanswered
Honi drew a circle, swore an oath to God, and insisted on rain that was neither drizzle nor destructive, but generous and blessing-filled
Rain fell in its proper measure until it flooded Jerusalem, and the people went up to the Temple Mount
The people ask Honi to pray for the rain to stop
Honi tells them to check whether the Claimants Stone has been washed away, a sign the flood is still too high
Shimon ben Shetah rebukes Honi, saying he would excommunicate him but that God obeys him like a son who nags his father
Supports the rebuke with the verse in Proverbs saying the parents should rejoice in the child
Mishnah: if rain falls before sunrise or midday the fast may end early; Rabbi Eliezer sets the cutoff at midday
Lod fasted, rain fell before midday, and Rabbi Tarfon told them to eat, drink and celebrate with the great Hallel
The Gemara recalls that the order of fasts applies to the first rainfall, as the mishna states
Raises a baraita that appears to contradict the mishna on when the third period without rain requires fasting
Rav Yehuda explains the mishna: fasting follows three missed rainy periods, but crying out is immediate when crops sprouted and then deteriorated
Rav Nachman limits the rule to crops whose appearance changed, and not to crops that dried out completely

Rav Nachman's ruling is needed for stalks that grew after drying out, which might otherwise seem salvageable
The mishna adds that forty days without rain between rainfalls also calls for crying out

Rabbi Yohanan limits this to times when money is cheap and produce dear; otherwise cry out immediately
Rabbi Yohanan recalls a time when grain was cheap yet people starved in Tiberias, showing the point
Mishna: if rain suffices for vegetation but not trees, or for both but not for cisterns, cry out immediately
Gemara shows how each partial rain case can occur, such as gentle or heavy rain alone affecting only some crops
Objects that the case of rain filling cisterns but not trees is hard to find, and cites a baraita
The baraita teaches that rain can fill cisterns, ditches and caves yet not benefit trees or vegetation
Asks how such a case, filling cisterns but not benefiting plants, could happen at all
It happens when rain comes in one heavy downpour that fills cisterns but does not soak the soil
Baraita: cry out for trees until Passover and for cisterns until Sukkot, and at once if there is no drinking water
Explains that immediately means on Monday, Thursday and the following Monday after the court learns of the crisis
Such outcries apply only within the district affected, not across areas where rain falls normally
Diphtheria warrants an outcry only if it can cause death; the same logic applies to other plagues
Locusts warrant an outcry in any amount, since more are likely to follow
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says grasshoppers too warrant an outcry because they can cause great damage
Baraita: in the Sabbatical year cry out for cisterns and caves, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds trees for the poor
Another baraita repeats the Sabbatical rule and adds aftergrowth, since the poor eat it
Rabbi Elazar ben Perata says rain has been meager since the Temple's destruction, with four kinds of years
Analogy: a servant whose master gives his weekly bread on Sunday eats it properly, like rain falling on time
A year in which rain does not fall on time is the next category described
Analogy: a servant given his portion on Shabbat eve bakes and eats it improperly, like rain arriving late
A year of abundant rain is the next category described
Analogy: a servant given all his grain at once grinds it in one batch, so less is wasted and the flour keeps
A year of scarce rain is the next category described

Baraita: once all Israel went up to Jerusalem for a festival and had no water to drink, the story begins
Nakdimon ben Guryon borrows twelve wells of water from a gentile officer and promises either the water or twelve talents
The deadline arrives and no rain has fallen, so Nakdimon must repay the officer

Nakdimon replies that he still has time, since the whole day is his
At noon the officer repeats the demand for the water or the money
Nakdimon replies that he still has time left in the day
In the afternoon the officer again demands the water or the money
Nakdimon again says he still has time left in the day

ranges.en: Narrative: the rain falls and the official goes joyfully into the bathhouse

The twelve cisterns fill and overflow before the official leaves the bathhouse
Nakdimon asks the official to pay for the extra water that the rain supplied
The official says God shook the world only for Nakdimon's sake, but he still has a claim
The official maintains his claim: the sun had set on the due date, so the rain fell on his property
Nakdimon returns to the Temple, prays again, and asks God to reveal that He has beloved ones
The clouds immediately disperse and the sun shines at that moment
The official says that had the sun not broken through, he would have had grounds to collect his coins
A Sage teaches that Nakdimon was really named Buni, and was called Nakdimon because the sun broke through for him
Three people had the sun shine at an irregular time for them: Moses, Joshua and Nakdimon ben Guryon
Joshua's miracle is supported by the verse in Joshua where the sun stood still

Rabbi Elazar derives it by a verbal analogy on the word I will begin, linking Moses and Joshua
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani derives it by a verbal analogy on the word put, linking Moses and Joshua
Rabbi Yohanan derives it from the verse itself, since the nations trembled when the sun broke through for Moses
Mishna: a city on which rain did not fall while the surrounding area had rain is under divine curse
Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav, says both cities face a curse, one in drought and one in destructive storms
Supports the claim with the Lamentations verse saying Jerusalem was among them like a menstruating woman
Rav reads the menstruating-woman verse as a blessing: Jerusalem, like a woman, can be made permitted again
Cites the Lamentations verse on Jerusalem becoming like a widow
Rav Yehuda reads the widow verse as a blessing: she is like a wife whose husband is abroad and intends to return
Cites the Malachi verse saying God made Israel contemptible and base
Rav Yehuda reads the Malachi verse as a blessing: the nations do not appoint Jews as river or government officials
Cites the verse from Kings that God will smite Israel as a reed is shaken in water
Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav, reads the reed verse as a blessing
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quotes Rabbi Yonatan that the curse of Ahijah is stronger than Balaam's blessing
Asks what the meaning of the verse in Proverbs is
Cites the Proverbs verse about the wounds of a friend and the deceitful kisses of an enemy
Explains the verse: Ahijah's curse of Israel is more effective than the blessing Balaam gave them
Ahijah cursed Israel by comparing them to a reed, saying it is said to them
Cites the verse that God will smite Israel as a reed is shaken
Rabbi Yohanan explains the reed's qualities: it stands in water, regrows and survives every wind, so Israel will survive
Balaam, by contrast, blessed Israel by comparing them to a cedar
Cites the verse from Numbers comparing Israel to cedars beside the waters

Teaching: a person should always be soft like a reed and not stiff like a cedar

20b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Narrative: an extremely ugly man greets Rabbi Elazar, who does not return the greeting
Rabbi Elazar insults the man, calling him worthless and asking how ugly he is
Rabbi Elazar asks whether all the people of the man's city are as ugly as he is
The man replies that he does not know, and tells Rabbi Elazar to say to the Craftsman: how ugly is this vessel you made
Rabbi Elazar realizes his sin, dismounts, prostrates himself and asks the man to forgive him
Rabbi Elazar requests forgiveness from the man
The man refuses until Rabbi Elazar goes to the Craftsman and says the same words about the vessel
Rabbi Elazar follows the man, trying to appease him, until they reach his city
The townspeople come out to greet Rabbi Elazar with titles of honor, and the man asks them about it
The man asks whom they are calling rabbi and master
The townspeople say they are calling the man who walks behind him
The man says that if this is a rabbi, there should not be many like him in Israel
The townspeople ask why he says this
He explains that Rabbi Elazar treated him that way
The townspeople plead that Rabbi Elazar is a great Torah scholar, so he should be forgiven
The man forgives him for their sake, on condition that he not become accustomed to such behavior
Rabbi Elazar immediately teaches that a person should be soft like a reed, not stiff like a cedar
Mishna: the same applies to a city afflicted by pestilence or by collapsing buildings
Baraita: the Sages referred only to sturdy walls not ready to fall, not to dilapidated walls ready to fall
Asks what exactly sturdy, not ready to fall, dilapidated and ready to fall walls are, since the baraita seems repetitive
Two cases are distinguished: walls that fall due to excess height, or walls set on an unstable riverbank
Rav and Shmuel avoided a dilapidated wall in Neharde'a that stood thirteen years, until Rav Adda bar Ahava arrived
Shmuel asks Rav to come with him and walk around the wall so they do not stand beneath it
Rav says this is unnecessary today, as Rav Adda bar Ahava is with them and his merit is great
Rav Huna needed to move wine from a dilapidated house, so he kept Rav Adda talking in halakha until it was all out
The house collapses just after they leave, and Rav Adda realizes what happened and becomes angry
Explains his anger: Rabbi Yannai taught not to stand in danger expecting a miracle, since miracles are deducted from one's merits
Rav Hanan asks what verse alludes to this idea
Cites the verse from Genesis: I am diminished by all the mercies and truth You showed Your servant
Asks what were the deeds of Rav Adda bar Ahava that brought him long life
Relates that Rav Adda's students asked him, or Rabbi Zeira's students asked him, about his longevity
The students ask to what he attributes his long life
He never raged at his household, never walked ahead of a greater man, and never slept in the study hall or mocked his colleagues
Rava asks Rafram bar Pappa to tell some of Rav Huna's fine deeds
Rafram recalls Rav Huna's old-age deeds: he surveyed the city on cloudy days and had unstable walls torn down or rebuilt
Every Shabbat eve Rav Huna bought the unsold vegetables from gardeners and threw them into the river
Asks why he did not simply give the vegetables to the poor
If he did, the poor would rely on his handouts and stop buying, ruining the gardeners' livelihood
Asks why he did not feed the vegetables to the animals
Rav Huna holds that human food may not be given to animals, as that displays contempt for the food
If he could not use the vegetables, he should not have bought them at all
Otherwise he would cause a stumbling block: sellers would stop bringing enough produce for Shabbat
Rav Huna hung a jug of new medicine by his door and invited anyone in need, an alternative account of a remedy for a demon
Rav Huna opened his door and invited anyone to eat; Rava says he can fulfill all these customs except this last one

21a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continuing the earlier story, Ilfa and Rabbi Yohanan decide to go into business to support themselves
Cites the verse that there should be no needy among you to justify their decision to work
They sit under a dilapidated wall; Rabbi Yohanan overhears two angels planning to topple it on them
The other angel replies to leave them, since one of them still has his time of achievement ahead
Ilfa did not hear the angels; Rabbi Yohanan infers that it is he whose achievement time has come
Rabbi Yohanan resolves to return to study and fulfill the verse on the poor for himself
Cites the verse that the poor shall never cease from the land to support his return to study
Rabbi Yohanan returns to the study hall, while Ilfa goes into business and Rabbi Yohanan becomes head of the academy
Ilfa's colleagues object that had he studied instead of going into business, he would have become head of the academy
Ilfa hangs himself from a ship's mast, vowing to fall into the sea if he cannot answer a baraita question from a mishna
An old man teaches a baraita: a dying man's instruction to give a shekel weekly lets the court give a sela if needs require
The baraita continues: if the father says heirs should take over, the court gives only a shekel per week
Ilfa asks in accordance with whose opinion this ruling is
It is Rabbi Meir's view that it is a mitzva to fulfill the statement of the dead
Describes Nahum of Gam Zu's suffering: blind, limbless, covered in boils, lying in a dilapidated house with bed legs in water
He tells his students to remove the vessels first and his bed last, guaranteeing the house stands while he is in it
The students ask why, if he is wholly righteous, such suffering befell him
He explains that he caused it himself: a poor man asked him for food on the road, and he died before he could give it
He cursed his own eyes, hands and legs, and wished his whole body be covered in boils to atone for his failure
The students lament that they have seen him in this state
He replies that it would be worse had they not seen him, since this suffering atones for him
Asks why he was called Nahum of Gam Zu
He would say about every event: this too is for the good, which is the source of his name
The Jews send Nahum of Gam Zu with a chest of jewels as a gift for the emperor
At an inn the residents steal the jewels and fill the chest with earth; Nahum says this too is for the good
At the palace the chest is opened and found full of earth, and the king plans to execute the Jewish emissaries
The king thinks the Jews are mocking him
Nahum again says this too is for the good
Elijah, disguised as a minister, suggests the earth is from the earth of their father Abraham
Abraham's earth turned into swords and arrows when he threw it, explaining the earth's power
Cites the verse from Isaiah that God's sword makes them as dust and His bow as driven stubble
A province the Romans could not conquer was taken by testing this earth on enemies
The emperor fills Nahum's chest with precious stones and sends him off with great honor
The residents ask what he brought that earned such honor
He says he took from here and brought it there, so they conclude their inn's soil is miraculous
The innkeepers tear down the inn and bring its soil to the king, but it has no power; he executes them
Mishna: a city sending out five hundred infantrymen with three deaths on consecutive days is a plague of pestilence
Baraita: for a city of fifteen hundred, like Akko, nine deaths over three days count, but not all in one day
For a city of five hundred, like Amiko, three deaths on three consecutive days count as a plague

21b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna continued: if all three died on one day or over four days, this is not a plague of pestilence
Example of Drokart, a city of five hundred infantrymen where three died in one day
Rav Nachman bar Rav Hisda decreed a fast on account of that plague
Rav Nachman bar Yitzhak asks in accordance with whose opinion the fast was declared
It must be Rabbi Meir's view, who treats separated goring as forewarning, and so a single day should suffice
Rav Nachman bar Rav Hisda invites Rav Nachman bar Yitzhak to come and lead their community
He declines, citing Rabbi Yosei that a person honors the place, not the place the person
Supports this with the Sinai case, where the sanctity of the mountain depended on the Divine Presence resting there
Supports it with the Tent of Meeting, whose site was sacred only while the Presence was there
Rav Nachman bar Rav Hisda proposes that he come to Rav Nachman bar Yitzhak to learn Torah
It is better that a lesser scholar come to the greater, not the reverse, since one is the son of a scholar and the other is not
In Sura a plague spared Rav's neighborhood, but a dream shows it was due to a man who lent his burial tools
In Drokart a fire spared Rav Huna's neighborhood, but a dream shows it was due to a woman who lent her oven
Locusts came to Rav Yehuda's region and he decreed a fast
The people object that the locusts are not destroying anything, since they eat only a little
Rav Yehuda replies that they will surely eat the crops later, as they have brought no provisions
Pestilence among pigs is reported to Rav Yehuda, who decreed a fast
The Gemara asks: does Rav Yehuda hold that a plague affecting one species spreads to all species
No, pigs are different, since their intestines resemble those of humans, so their disease might spread to people
Pestilence in Bei Hozai is reported to Shmuel, who decreed a fast in Babylonia
They object that Bei Hozai is far from Babylonia
Shmuel replies that there is no barrier here to stop the pestilence from reaching them
Pestilence in Eretz Yisrael is reported to Rav Nachman, who decreed a fast in Babylonia
Rav Nachman reasons: if the lady, Eretz Yisrael, is afflicted, all the more so the maidservant, Babylonia
The Gemara infers that a maidservant and a maidservant, two Diaspora places, would not warrant a fast
But Shmuel decreed a fast for Neharde'a regarding pestilence in Bei Hozai, which is not a lady relative to it
It is different there, because caravans travel regularly from Bei Hozai to Neharde'a and could carry the pestilence
Abba the Bloodletter received greetings from the heavenly yeshiva daily, unlike Abaye and Rava, which troubled Abaye
He was told that Abaye could not do what Abba did, and so did not merit the same honor
Asks what the deeds of Abba the Bloodletter were
He separated men and women in treatment, used a garment with a slit, and took fees privately so no one was embarrassed
For a Torah scholar he took no fee and gave money for healthy food afterward
Abaye sent two Sages to test him; he fed them, gave them drink and spread mats for them at night

22a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: In the morning the Sages took Abba's rugs and carried them to the market, where Abba found them
The Sages ask Abba to appraise how much the rugs are worth
Abba gives his price and says that is what he paid, and insists he will not sell for more
The Sages say the rugs are his and they took them from him
The Sages ask what Abba suspected them of when he did not object
Abba explains he assumed they needed money to ransom captives and were too embarrassed to ask, so he gave the rugs to charity
Rava was distressed that Abaye received greetings from Heaven every Shabbat eve while he received them only on Yom Kippur eve
They consoled him that through his merit he protects his entire city
Rabbi Beroka Hoza'a often walked in the market of Bei Lefet, where Elijah the Prophet would appear to him
Rabbi Beroka asks Elijah whether anyone in this market is worthy of the World-to-Come
Elijah says no
Beroka then sees a man in black shoes without ritual fringes, whom Elijah identifies as worthy, so Beroka runs after him
Beroka asks the man what his occupation is
The man asks him to go away now and return the next day
On the next day Beroka asks again what his occupation is
He is a prison guard who separates men from women and risks his life saving a betrothed woman by staining her dress
Beroka asks why he lacks ritual fringes and wears black shoes
He dresses to pass among gentiles unnoticed, and when they decree, he informs the Sages, who pray and annul the decree
Beroka asks why the man said come tomorrow when he was first asked
He recounts that he had told Beroka to come back tomorrow
At that moment a decree had just been issued, so he first had to inform the Sages to pray for mercy
Elijah says two brothers who appear in the market also have a share in the World-to-Come
Beroka asks the brothers what their occupation is
They are jesters who cheer the depressed and make peace between quarrelling people, earning reward in this world and the next
Mishna: for the following calamities they sound the alarm in every place
Baraita lists the calamities; Rabbi Akiva says that for locusts a single wing seen in Eretz Yisrael suffices
Mishna: for dangerous beasts they also sound the alarm
Baraita: they sound the alarm for a dangerous beast only if it is an outbreak, not otherwise
The Gemara asks what counts as an outbreak and what does not
A beast seen in town or by day is an outbreak; in the field or at night it is not, and similarly for chasing or hiding
Baraita continues: a beast that tears two people and eats one, or climbs a roof to take a baby, counts as an outbreak
The Gemara asks why the baraita seems to say both day and night, and then distinguishes by day and by night
This is not difficult: in town by day is an outbreak and in town by night is not, while in the field the reverse applies
The Gemara asks about a second apparent contradiction on whether standing or running away marks an outbreak
Near a marsh the beast can run into it, so standing is natural; far from one, standing shows unnatural lack of fear
The baraita says a beast that eats both people is not an outbreak
The Gemara asks: but did you not say even chasing two people is an outbreak
Rav Pappa replies that the ruling about eating one refers to a beast in a marsh, its own habitat
The Gemara asks why the baraita states the obvious case of a beast taking a baby from its cradle
Rav Pappa replies that it refers to a hunter's hut roof, where one might think the attack is natural
Mishna: for the sword they sound the alarm
Baraita: the sword includes even a sword of peace, an army merely passing through, as Pharaoh Neco shows, since King Josiah was harmed

22b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Scripture quoted: Necho sent envoys saying he was not coming against Judah, so Josiah should not interfere
What does the phrase God who is with me mean
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, says it refers to Necho's idol; Josiah reasoned he could beat a king who trusts in idols
Scripture quoted: the archers shot King Josiah and he asked to be moved away because he was badly wounded
What does I am seriously wounded mean
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, explains that the archers made his whole body as full of holes as a sieve
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani reports a teaching of Rabbi Yohanan
Why was Josiah punished
Because he should have consulted Jeremiah and did not
What did the Sages derive from this
Scripture quoted: the sword shall not pass through your land
What is meant by sword
If the sword means one not of peace, that contradicts the verse promising peace in the land
Rather, even a sword of peace is meant, and Josiah did not realize his generation did not merit that protection
Jeremiah saw Josiah's lips moving and feared he was speaking improperly, but heard him justify God's judgment
Josiah accepts God's judgment in words of Lamentations, saying God is righteous
At that moment Jeremiah began his lament over Josiah
Scripture quoted from Lamentations as Jeremiah's eulogy for the anointed king
An incident: elders went down from Jerusalem to their cities and declared a fast
Did the fast refer to enough grain to fill an oven, or enough to make bread to fill an oven
The Gemara cites the mishna's wording of enough to fill the mouth of an oven as a source
The dilemma remains: is it the bread covering the oven or a row around its mouth; left unresolved
The mishna: they also decreed a fast because wolves had eaten children
Ulla cites Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak on an incident where wolves swallowed children and the Sages ruled on purity
The mishna continues: for these cases the alarm is sounded even on Shabbat
A baraita lists the cases for sounding alarm, and says an individual may fast to avert evil decrees
Rabbi Yosei disagrees: an individual may not fast, lest he become dependent on others who will not pity him
What is the reason for Rabbi Yosei's view
His reason is the verse about man becoming a living soul, read as a duty to preserve life
Shimon the Temanite says one may cry out even about pestilence
Did the Sages disagree only on Shabbat, or entirely, and did they agree on weekdays
A baraita is cited: one cries out about such matters on Shabbat, all the more so on weekdays
Rabbi Hanan ben Pitom, citing Rabbi Akiva, says one does not cry out about pestilence at all
The mishna: one sounds the alarm for any calamity coming upon the community
A baraita: the alarm is sounded for any calamity except an excess of rain
What is the reason
Rabbi Yohanan explains: one does not pray against an excess of good
Rabbi Yohanan asks where this is derived from
Scripture quoted from Malachi: bring the tithe and I will pour out a blessing
What does until there is more than enough mean
Rami bar Hama explains the abundance will wear out the lips from saying enough
Rami bar Rav Yud says the rule applies in Eretz Yisrael, but in the Diaspora they do cry out over excess rain
A baraita supports the Diaspora practice: the priestly watch asked the others to pray for brethren in the Diaspora
They asked Rabbi Eliezer how much rain must fall before they stop praying for it
He answered hyperbolically: enough that a person can stand in a deep cliff and dip his feet in water
A baraita says hands and feet are treated alike, so his answer should mention hands
Rabbi Eliezer's answer stands: I meant feet like hands
Rabba bar bar Hana reports he personally saw the cliff and an Arab rider below looked like a worm
A baraita cites the verse: I will give your rains in their season
Rain should be moderate: excess rain muddies the soil so it yields no produce; an alternative explanation follows

23a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: In its season is explained as Wednesday evenings and Shabbat evenings, when people stay indoors
In the time of Shimon ben Shetah rain fell at those times, so crops grew huge, a lesson for later generations
The purpose of the example is to show how much sin harms the world
Jeremiah 5:24-25 is quoted: sins withhold the good rain from you
In Herod's time rain fell only at night while they built the Temple, showing that Heaven's work was done by their hands
The mishna refers to the incident in which people sent for Honi the circle-drawer
Baraita: late in Adar no rain fell, they asked Honi to pray, he prayed and still nothing fell
Honi drew a circle and sat inside it, the same way the prophet Habakkuk did
Habakkuk 2:1 is quoted to support the idea that Habakkuk stood on his watch
Honi tells God that his people turned to him as one of the household, and swears he will not move until God has mercy
Rain began to fall as a drizzle
His students object: this small rain only dissolves his oath and will not save them
Honi replies that he asked for rain to fill cisterns, ditches and caves
Rain then fell in torrents, each drop the size of a barrel mouth, and the Sages estimated no drop was under a log
The students object again: this rain is so heavy it will destroy the world
Honi replies that he asked for rain of favor, blessing and generosity, which fell in its proper measure
Because of the rain, all the people went up to the Temple Mount
His students ask him to pray for the rain to stop, just as he prayed for it to fall
Honi explains that the tradition is not to pray for an excess of good
Nevertheless Honi asks for a thanksgiving bull to be brought
Honi prays that the rains stop; the wind blows, clouds clear, and people go out and find truffles and mushrooms
Shimon ben Shetah rebukes Honi: he would excommunicate him, since God's name is profaned through him
Honi replies with a parable: like a child who asks his father for what he wants, God grants his request
Proverbs 23:25 is quoted: let your father and mother rejoice
Baraita: the sons of the Chamber of Hewn Stone sent for Honi the circle-drawer
Job 22:28 is quoted: you shall decree a thing and it shall be established for you
The verse is explained: what you decree from below, God fulfills from above
The verse is applied to Honi: God lifts up those who are humble and saves those who are lowly
The verse is applied to Honi: God saves the one who is not clean through prayer, and delivers through the works of the hands
Rabbi Yohanan says that righteous man was always distressed by the verse of Psalm 126
Psalm 126:1 is quoted: when the Lord returned the captivity of Zion, we were like dreamers
Can anyone sleep seventy years in a dream
A story: one day a man was walking and saw someone planting a carob tree
He asks how many years it takes until it bears fruit
The planter says it takes seventy years
The traveler tells him he must have slept seventy years, since that is obvious
The planter replies that he found the world full of carob trees, planted by his fathers, so he plants for his children
The traveler sat eating bread, fell asleep, and slept seventy years with his eyes covered
On waking he saw a man gathering carobs from the tree
He asks whether that man is the one who planted it
The man says he is the grandson of the planter
The traveler concludes that he must have slept seventy years
He saw his donkey, and a foal had been born with a saddle, and he went home
He asks whether Honi the circle-drawer's son is still alive
They tell him the son is not alive, but the grandson is
He declares that he is Honi the circle-drawer, but they did not believe him
He went to the study hall, heard the Sages reciting traditions, and they were clear like those of Honi
He resolved every difficulty the Sages had, but they did not believe him or honor him as he deserved
He became distressed, prayed for mercy, and died
Rava says this is what people mean by either companionship or death
Abba Helkiah, the grandson of Honi, was asked by the Sages to pray for rain when it was needed, and rain came
Once the world needed rain, a pair of Sages went to him to ask him to pray for rain to come
They did not find him at home; they found him in the field, and they greeted him with peace

23b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Honi did not return the greetings of the Sages who approached him
Honi carried wood and tools, went barefoot, and on reaching home his finely dressed wife came out to greet him; he sat and ate
Honi did not invite the Sages to eat; he broke the bread and gave one portion to the older child and two to the younger
Honi tells his wife that the Sages came because of the rain
Honi proposes they go up to the roof and pray, so that rain comes without them taking credit for it
They went up; Honi stood in one corner and his wife in another, and the clouds moved from her corner and rain fell
Honi asks why the Sages came
The Sages say they were sent to ask him to pray for rain
Honi says God is blessed for not needing the Sages to ask Abba Helkiah for rain
The Sages ask him to explain the strange things they noticed, such as why he did not return their greeting
Honi explains that he was a day laborer and would not delay his work
Why did he carry the tools and cloak as he did
He carried one load on one shoulder and his cloak on the other
The cloak was borrowed: he borrowed it for one purpose and did not borrow it for another
Why did he walk the whole road without his shoes
When he reached water he put on his shoes, and he explained this to them
Why did he see nothing along the way in the water
When Honi reached the city, he told them what he saw
He explains that one thing is a long advantage and the other is not an advantage
What is the reason
When Honi reached the city, his wife came out to greet him, dressed up
He explains that he did not want to set his eyes on another woman
What is the reason
His wife entered first, then he entered after her, and then the Sages entered
He answers that they had not properly examined him, so he explained his conduct
What is the reason
When he broke bread he did not invite the Sages to eat with him
The bread was not plentiful, and he did not want to give his bread to the Sages for free
What is the reason
He gave one portion to the older child and two to the younger
One of them stands in the house while the other sits in the synagogue
What is the reason
The cloud rose from his wife's corner because she often gave bread to the poor, while he only gave a coin
Alternatively, he prayed that the troublemakers in their houses would die, while she prayed that they would repent
She prayed that they would return to repentance, and they did repent
Hanan the Hidden, son of Honi's daughter, lived when the world needed rain and the Sages sent children to him
The children held the hem of his cloak and asked him for rain
The children beg him to give them rain now
He prayed that God act for the sake of these children, who cannot tell the rain-giver from the one who does not give rain
Why was he called Hanan the Hidden
Because he hid himself in the bathhouse
Rabbi Zeriqa tells Rav Safra to come and see how the pious men of Israel differ from those of Babylonia
The Babylonian pious men, Rav Huna and Rav Hisda, said they would gather together and pray for God to bring rain
An example from the Land of Israel is Rabbi Yona, the father of Rabbi Mani
When the world needed rain, Rabbi Yona went home, asked for his wraps, and went out to stand in a deep place
Psalm 130:1 is quoted: out of the depths I have called to You, O Lord
He stood in a hidden place covered with sackcloth and prayed for mercy, and rain came
When he came home, the people told him to bring them food
He says that since rain has come and the world is relieved, there was no need to bring food
Rabbi Mani's son, harassed by the household of the Nasi, prostrated himself at his father's grave and complained that they harass him
One day riders passed by; he grabbed their horses' feet until they agreed to stop harassing him
Rabbi Mani was often in the presence of Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elishiv
He said that the wealthy people of his household see that they harass him
He said: let them ask, and they were answered
He said they press him; he said let them be granted, and they were granted; he said his household does not accept him
A story about a woman named Hannah: she beautified herself, then returned to her former state after he rebuked her
Two students who were before Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elishiv ask him to pray that they become very wise
He said that she is my people and I sent her away
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin was often before Rabbi Yosei of Yokrat, then left him and came before Rav Ashi

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: One day Shmuel heard someone studying a teaching
Shmuel rules that one who pulls a fish from the sea on Shabbat is liable once it dries, if it is worth a sela
Objection: then the master should also hold liable for the fins, which contradicts his ruling
The view in that case is attributed to Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Avin
He replies that he himself is the one who said it
Was the master not often before Rabbi Yosei of Yokrat
Yes, he was
Why then did the master leave him and come here
He says a man who wronged his own family showed no mercy to him, so how could he show mercy to his son
What is this
A story: laborers in the desert were hired, and he did not bring them bread
The laborers said to his son that they were hungry, and sat under a fig tree
He told the fig tree to bring out its fruit so the laborers could eat, and it did so right away
His father told them not to think he had done this for a commandment, since the fig was still plentiful
The laborers blessed him that the Merciful One would satisfy him as he satisfied them
Where do you know this from
They say that such a thing happened
His father rebukes him: you made your Creator work to bring out figs out of season
His daughter was a beautiful girl
One day she saw a man who was a healthy outdoor worker, and he looked at her
What is this
The man says: if I cannot marry her, I will not even get to see her
The father tells his daughter that she is troubling people, so she should return to her dust before people stumble over her
A donkey driver's wife would send out her pay each evening and bring it home, unless they harmed her
One day people put on her shoes, and she would not go until they took them off her
Elazar of Birta gave away everything he had when the charity collectors came to him
One day he went to the market to buy a dowry for his daughter, and the charity collectors saw him
The collectors took everything from him, and he ran after them
He asks them, by oath, what they are doing with the money
They say it is for an orphan and a widow; he replies that their need comes before his daughters
He took everything he had and gave it to them
He had one coin left, bought wheat with it, and put it in a basket
His wife came and asked her daughter what their father had brought
What did your father bring
She said everything he brought he threw in the basket, and she came to open the basket door
She saw the basket full of wheat, coming out through the tube of the threshing floor, and could not open the door
The daughter went to the study hall and said: come and see what your beloved did to you
He replies that these are consecrated and you have a share like any poor Israelite
Rabbi Yehuda the Patriarch decreed a fast and prayed for rain, but no rain came
He says: how many more were there than Shmuel? I raised up Yehuda ben Gamliel; woe to the generation that stumbles
Woe to him who lived in his days; he became distressed, and rain came
The Patriarch's household decreed a fast without informing Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish until morning
Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yohanan: did we not accept the fast upon ourselves the night before
Rabbi Yohanan replies that we follow after the Patriarch's household
The Patriarch's household decreed a fast and no rain came
Ushaya the Younger of the associates taught them
Numbers 15:24 is quoted: if it was done in error by the eyes of the congregation
A parable: a bride in her father house needs no full inspection while her eyes are beautiful, but does when they are dull
Servants came and put a cloth around his neck to harass him, and the people said to let him be, since he also harasses us
Since all his words are for the sake of heaven, they said nothing to him and left him alone
Rabbi declared a fast and no rain came
Ilfa went down before the ark, and they said to him: Rabbi, Ilfa
Ilfa said: He who makes the wind blow and the wind rise, who brings down the rain, and rain came
He asks him: what is your work
He lives in a poor alley without wine for kiddush and havdalah, so he works to bring wine for others to fulfill their duty
Rav came to a certain place, declared a fast, and no rain came; the messenger of the congregation came down before him
The messenger said: He who makes the wind blow, the wind rose, and he said: He who brings down the rain, and rain came
He asks him: what is your work
He teaches poor and rich children alike, takes nothing from those who cannot pay, and drills the negligent until they learn
Rav Nahman declared a fast, prayed for mercy, and no rain came
They said to take Nahman and throw him from the wall to the ground; his mind was distressed, and rain came
Rabbah declared a fast and prayed for mercy, and no rain came
They objected: but when Rav Yehuda declared a fast, rain came
Rabbah replies: what can I do? If it depends on fasting, we are greater than them, since all of Rav Yehuda's fasts

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara notes that we were teaching the six orders of the Mishnah in the Nezikin context
When Rav Yehuda reached the Oketzin mishna about a woman pickling vegetables and olives, he declared them ritually pure
Rav and Shmuel's view is found here, while we are teaching the thirteen Oketzin rulings
When Rav Yehuda removed a sandal, rain came, and we kept crying out all day for rain
No one paid attention, and the great men of the generation are not like the earlier ones
Rav Yehuda saw two households breaking bread and concluded there was hunger in the world, so the Sages told him
The Sages asked Rav Kahana, son of Rav Nehunya, to make him go out to the market near the gate, where he saw a crowd
He asks what this is
They say it is a pile of date palms being sold
He concludes there is a general famine in the world
He told his servant to take off his sandal, and one sandal was removed and rain came
When he went to remove the second sandal, Elijah came and spoke to him
Elijah says God declared that if he removes the other sandal, He will destroy the world
Rav Mari, son of Shmuel's daughter, reports he saw angels disguised as salters bringing salt; they warned people not to buy the flour
This was a miracle, and the next day they came to the flour warehouse
Rava came to Hagronia, declared a fast, and no rain came, so he told the people to fast again the next day
He asks who saw a dream and should tell it
Rabbi Elazar of Hagronia says he dreamed it
The dream conveys a good greeting to Rav: good is the Master, who is good to His people
He concludes it is a time of favor, so they should pray for mercy, and rain came
A man was flogged in Rava court for relations with a Samaritan woman and died; the news reached the king Shapur
The king wanted to harm Rava; his mother Ifra Hormiz told him not to meddle with the Jews, since their prayers are answered
He asks her: what is it
She says they pray for rain and it came
He tells her it is because it is the rainy season
Rather, let them pray now in the Tammuz solstice that rain should come
She sent word to Rava to direct his mind and pray for rain; he prayed, but no rain came
He prayed to his Master in heaven
Psalm 44:2 is quoted: we heard with our ears what our fathers told us, but in our eyes we did not see
Rain came
It came until the gutters of Tzipori overflowed into the Diglat river
His father appeared to him in a dream and said to him
Is there anyone who troubles heaven so much
He says your place and his place are different
The next day, Rav Pappa found him stripping at the knives; Rav Pappa declared a fast and no rain came
His heart became weak; he ate a plate of porridge, prayed for mercy, and no rain came
Rav Nahman bar Ushpizai said: if you eat another plate of porridge, rain will come; he became embarrassed and distressed, and rain came
Hanina ben Dosa, walking on the road, prayed that the world be at ease while he suffered, and the rain stopped
When he came home he said: all the world is distressed but Hanina is comfortable, and the rain came
Rav Yosef asks what the high priest's prayer accomplished compared with Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
A mishna is quoted: he would pray a brief prayer in the outer chamber
What did they pray
Rabin bar Ada and Rava bar Ada both say in the name of Rav Yehuda
The prayer: may this year be rainy rather than dry, since dryness is not good; let the travelers prayers not enter before You
Rav Aha son of Rava concludes in Rav Yehuda name: the ruler does not act arbitrarily, and Your people should support one another
A heavenly voice declares daily that the world is fed for the sake of Hanina my son, who needs one kav of carobs weekly
His wife used to light the oven every Friday evening and cast the lamp

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A story about a bad neighbor woman whose bread was burning, and she went out to the courtyard where a miracle was done for her
The neighbor says to the woman: bring the tool, your bread is burning, and she explains that she entered for this reason
The woman entered because she was used to miracles; she asked her husband how long they would suffer, and he prayed for mercy
A hand-like thing came out and they gave him a golden table leg; in a dream he saw the righteous eating at a golden table
In the dream the righteous will eat at a table with two legs, and everyone else at the complete table
The woman says they eat at a table that is lacking
And what shall we do
He prayed that they be taken from her, and they were taken
The last miracle was greater than the first, since what is given is not taken back
One of the attendants saw his daughter who was sad
He asks her: my daughter, why are you sad
She says that a vessel of vinegar got mixed with her oil, and she lit from it for Shabbat
He replies: whoever said to the oil to burn will say to the vinegar to burn, so do not worry
The lamp kept burning all day until they took light from it for havdalah
Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa had goats, and people told him they were damaging things
He said: if the goats damage, let bears eat them; if not, each goat should come home at night with a bear on its horns
A neighbor woman was building a house, and her beams did not reach, so she came before him
She complains that she built her house and her beams did not shrink to fit
He asks her: what is your name
She says her name is Eiko
He says: may your beams be shrunk
The beams reached the point where they extended a cubit in each direction; some say they were made as sniffing devices
Palimo reports seeing a house whose beams extended a cubit each way; he was told Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa built it by prayer
Where did Hanina get goats
But he was poor, and moreover the Sages said one may not raise small livestock in Eretz Yisrael
The Sages said one may not raise small livestock in Eretz Yisrael
Rav Pappa tells a story: a man left chickens at the door of Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa's wife
He told her not to eat their eggs; the chickens multiplied and they sold them and bought goats with the money
Once that man passed, and the chickens he had lost were gone; he told a friend he had left his chickens here
Hanina said to him: do you have a sign for them
He gave him a sign, and he took the goats, which were the goats that had come with bears on their horns
These are the goats that came with bears on their horns
Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat was deeply troubled and had nothing to eat, so he put a cloth in his mouth, grew weak, and fell asleep
The Sages came to visit him and saw him weeping and laughing, and a spark of fire came out of his mouth
When he woke, the spark of fire came from his mouth
They asked him: why did you cry and laugh
He told them: I was sitting with God, and they said to Him: how long shall I suffer in this world
God told me: Elazar my son, do you want Me to turn the world upside down from the beginning
They said before Him that perhaps he was born at the hour of sustenance; they said: he lives longer, or we live
God said: you have lived; they said before Him: if so, I do not want it
God says: for this reward I will give you in the world to come thirteen rivers of oil, balsam, pure spices, and Kafrat and Diglat
They said before Him: this, and nothing more; God said: to me and to your friend, what shall I give
They said: from a man who has nothing, I want to be revived with the Askatla
He spoke to Elazar with a playful remark about the convert
Rabbi Hama bar Hanina declared a fast and no rain came
They objected: but Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi declared a fast and rain came
He replied: here I am, the son of a Levite; I am not special
They said: let us come and direct our minds; is it possible the public's hearts were broken
Rain would come if they prayed, but rain did not come
He asks them: is it pleasing to you that rain should come on our account
They said: yes
He said: firmament, cover your face; when the firmament face was covered, rain came
Levi declared a fast, and no rain came
He said before God: You ascended and sat on high, and You do not have mercy on Your children; rain came
Rabbi Elazar said: one should never speak against Heaven, since a great man spoke against Heaven
Levi, with a bow before Rabbi, and Rabbi Hiyya bar Luliyani, and the rest of the story
He heard the clouds saying: let them go and water the lands of Ammon and Moab; he said before God, Master of the Universe
When You gave the Torah to Israel and other nations rejected it, and now You give them rain, send it here
Rabbi Hiyya bar Luliyani expounded the verse: what is written
Psalm 92:13 is quoted: the righteous will flourish like a palm tree and grow like a cedar in Lebanon
Why is palm mentioned and why cedar; if the verse said palm only, one would say palm; the wording is explained

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The cedar's trunk does not change, and neither does the trunk of the righteous, Heaven forbid
This explains why the verse mentions both palm and cedar: the cedar bears no fruit, the palm does, and the righteous bear fruit
Objection: but the cedar's trunk does change
A baraita is cited: one who buys a tree for cutting cuts it at the stated height, and a cedar's trunk does not change
Here we are speaking of other kinds of cedar
Rabba bar Huna's teaching: there are ten kinds of cedar
Isaiah 41:19 is quoted to support the ten kinds of cedar
A baraita: Rabbi Eliezer decreed thirteen fasts for the community, and rain did not fall until the people went out and wept
Rabbi Eliezer went before the ark and recited twenty-four blessings, but he was not answered
Rabbi Akiva went after him and said: Our Father, our King, we have no king but You; for Your sake have mercy, and rain fell
The Sages murmured, and a heavenly voice said: not because one is greater, but because one forgives and the other does not
A baraita: until when should the rain fall and the community stop fasting; Rabbi Meir and the Sages give different amounts of rain
A baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says no handbreadth rises above without a deep rising to meet it, three handbreadths
But it is taught two handbreadths
No contradiction: one is for cultivated land and one for uncultivated land
Rabbi Elazar says: when they pour the water at the festival, the deep says to its neighbor: let your waters flow
He says: I hear the sound of two friends
Psalm 42:8 is quoted: deep calls to deep at the sound of Your waterspouts
Rabba says he saw a vision: a creature like a calf, with its mouth open, standing between the lower deep and the upper deep
The upper deep said to the lower: let your waters flow; and the lower said: let your waters gurgle
Song of Songs 2:12 is quoted: the flowers appear in the land
Those who fast, and rain fell before sunrise, should not complete the fast
A baraita: those who fasted and rain fell before sunrise need not complete the fast; after sunrise they should complete it
Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yose each give a different hour after which one may complete the fast
For example, Ahab king of Israel fasted from the ninth hour onward
I Kings 21:29 is quoted: have you seen that Ahab has humbled himself before Me
Rabbi Yehuda the Patriarch decreed a fast, and rain fell after sunrise; he wanted to complete the fast
Rabbi Ami objects: we learned that a fast may be completed before noon but not after noon
Shmuel the Younger decreed a fast, and rain fell before sunrise
People thought it was praise for the community
Shmuel gives a parable: a servant asks his master for a gift; the master says to give it and not to listen to his voice
Again Shmuel the Younger decreed a fast, and rain fell after sunset; the people thought it was praise for the community
Shmuel said: it is not praise for the community; I will give you a parable
The parable continues: the master says to wait until the servant is wearied, then give it to him and to Shmuel
He says: He who makes the wind blow, and the wind blows; He who brings down the rain, and the rain came
An incident: they decreed a fast in Lod
Shall we say the Hallel from the beginning
Abaye and Rava both say: because they do not say Hallel on those days

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Is it so that Hallel is said over a satiated soul and full belly
Objection: Rav Pappa visited Abaye synagogue, declared a fast, rain fell until noon, and he then said Hallel and ate; Mahoza is different
The end-of-tractate formula, and the mishna opens: fasts are observed at three times a year
The mishna: priests lift their hands four times a day at fast-days, and on the watches and Yom Kippur
Numbers 28:2 is quoted: command the children of Israel, and say to them, My offering, My bread
How can a man's offering be brought if he does not stand over it
The early prophets established twenty-four watches, each with a standing group of priests, Levites and Israelites in Jerusalem
When a watch was due to go up, its priests and Levites went to Jerusalem while its Israelites gathered in their towns to read creation
The men of the standing group fasted four days a week, from Monday through Thursday, but not on Friday or Sunday
The creation account is read: first day, second day, and so on, until the heavens and earth were finished
The long passage is read by two people, the short one by one
In the morning, Musaf and Mincha they read by heart as with Shema on Friday evening; on Shabbat they did not enter at Mincha
There is no standing at morning service, no Musaf offering, no Neila offering, and no wood offering at Mincha
Rabbi Akiva's view, but Ben Azzai says: this is how Rabbi Yehoshua taught it
Rabbi Akiva went back to teaching as Ben Azzai taught it
The list of dates when the wood offering was brought: the first of Nisan, the twentieth of Tammuz, and the fifth of Av
Further dates for the wood offering: the seventh and tenth of the month and the fifteenth
The priests and Levites and the whole standing group, and whoever erred in his tribe, all had dates
Further dates: the twentieth, the twentieth of Elul, and the first of Tevet
The second Pharosh, on the first of Tevet, had no standing group, but Hallel, the Musaf offering and the wood offering were there
Five things happened to our fathers on the seventeenth of Tammuz and the ninth of Av

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The tablets were broken, the daily offering stopped, Jerusalem was breached on the Ninth of Av, and joy is reduced from the start of Av
If the Ninth of Av falls on Shabbat, one may not cut hair or wash clothes; on Thursday these are allowed out of honor for Shabbat
On the eve of the Ninth of Av one may not eat two cooked dishes, eat meat, or drink wine
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says Rabbi Yehuda required overturning the bed, but the Sages did not agree with him
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says there were no better days for Israel than the fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur, when maidens went out in borrowed white
The maidens used to sing: young man, look and choose; do not set your eyes on beauty but on family
Proverbs 31:30-31 is quoted: charm is deceptive and beauty is vain; a woman who fears the Lord shall be praised
And so it says
Song of Songs 3:11 is quoted and read as referring to the giving of the Torah and the building of the Temple
The mishna: priests lift their hands three times a year
Is Musaf missing from the list; this is how it is taught
The mishna restated: priests lift hands on any day they pray, some four times a day, and on fast days and Yom Kippur
Rav Nahman said in the name of Rabba bar Abuha: this is the view of Rabbi Meir
The Sages say that at Shacharit and Musaf there is hand lifting, but at Mincha and Neila there is no hand lifting
Who are the Sages? It is the view of Rabbi Yehuda
A baraita: Rabbi Meir says all four services have hand lifting; Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei each limit it to certain services
In what do they disagree; Rabbi Meir holds the reason every day is what
Priests did not lift their hands at Mincha because of drunkenness
Nowadays there is no drunkenness
Rabbi Yehuda holds that drunkenness is not common at Shacharit and Musaf, so no decree; but it is common at Mincha and Neila
Rabbi Yosei holds Mincha is held every day, so the Sages decreed it; Neila is not held every day, so no decree
Rav Yehuda said in Rav's name: the halakha follows Rabbi Meir; Rabbi Yohanan said the people have the custom to follow Rabbi Meir
Rava said: the custom follows Rabbi Meir
Clarifications: one who says the halakha follows Rabbi Meir expounds it in the chapter; one who says custom does not expound but teaches
Rav Nahman said: the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei, and again the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei
And nowadays, why do priests lift their hands at the Mincha of a fast
Because it is close to sunset, like Neila, and everyone is at least not drunk, a drunkard is forbidden from lifting hands
From where do we know this
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says in the name of bar Kapara: why is the section on the priestly blessing juxtaposed with the Nazirite section
To teach that just as a Nazirite is forbidden wine, so the priest who blesses is forbidden wine
Abba, father of Rabbi Zeira, or Ushaya bar Zavda, objects: if a Nazirite is forbidden grape skins, the priest who blesses should be too
Rabbi Yitzhak says the verse to serve Him and bless in His name shows: as a servant may eat grape skins, so may the blessing priest

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If a servant with a blemish may not serve, may a priest with a blemish not bless
Why compare to the Nazirite for leniency rather than for stringency
It is only a support from rabbinic law, and the comparison is for leniency
These are the standing groups
Numbers 28:2 is quoted: command the children of Israel
What is he saying
He means: these are the standing groups
And what is the reason the standing groups were established
Numbers 28:2 is quoted to show the basis for the standing groups
How can a man's offering be brought if he does not stand over it
The early prophets set twenty-four watches, each with a standing group of priests, Levites and Israelites in Jerusalem
A baraita: there were twenty-four watches in Eretz Yisrael and twelve in Jericho; half of a due watch went up to Jerusalem
The other half of the watch went up from Jericho to supply water and food for their brethren in Jerusalem
Rav Yehuda said in Shmuel's name: priests, Levites and Israelites are all required for the offering
A baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says priests, Levites and musical instruments are required for the offering
In what do they disagree
One holds the essence of song is with the mouth, and the other holds the essence of song is with instruments
Rav Hama bar Goria said in Rav name: Moses set eight watches, four from Eleazar and four from Itamar; Samuel set them at sixteen
David came and set them at twenty-four
I Chronicles 26:31 is quoted: in David fortieth year, mighty men of valor were sought out and found among them
Objection: Moses established eight watches, four from Eleazar and four from Itamar; David and Samuel then set them at twenty-four
I Chronicles 9:22 is quoted: David and Samuel founded them, the one who sees their faithfulness
This means: from the foundation laid by David and Samuel, Samuel the Ramathite set them at twenty-four
Another baraita: Moses established sixteen watches, eight from Eleazar and eight from Itamar
When the sons of Eleazar increased over the sons of Itamar, they divided them and set them at twenty-four
I Chronicles 24:4 is quoted: the sons of Eleazar had many leaders, so they divided sixteen houses for them and eight for Itamar
I Chronicles 24:6 is quoted: one house of fathers taken by Eleazar and one taken by Itamar
And if you say: just as the sons of Eleazar were many, so too the sons of Itamar were many
Originally there were eight, and they were four
Come and hear: one house of fathers taken by Eleazar and one taken by Itamar
This refutes Rav Hama bar Goria
Rav Hama bar Goria would say: it is a dispute among the tannaim
I say this is like the tanna who says eight
A baraita: four watches came up from the exile, and these are Yedayah, Harim, Pashhur and Immer, who stood among the prophets
