ranges.en: The mishna: priestly watches are divided by lot, and the watch's Israelites gather locally to read the Creation account.
The Gemara asks for the source of this practice and names the transmitter who supplies it.
Rav Asi teaches that heaven and earth endure only because of the non-priestly watches and the Temple service.
Rav Asi supports his teaching with a verse from Genesis 15 about Abraham asking how he will inherit the land.
Abraham fears Israel's sins will bring a flood-like destruction and asks God how he can be assured of inheriting the land.
God responds to Abraham's question.
God's reply cites the verse about the heifer, goat and ram, which are sacrificial animals.
Abraham asks what will happen to the people when no Temple stands to offer sacrifices.
God says the order of offerings is established, so reading them counts as sacrifice and sins are pardoned.
The baraita: the priestly watch prays for the offerings, while the other watch fasts Monday to Thursday for specific dangers, but not on Shabbat eve.
A fortiori argument: if one does not fast on Shabbat eve, certainly one does not fast on Shabbat itself.
Asks why they would not fast on Sunday.
Rabbi Yohanan: Sunday is avoided because of the Christians, for whom it is the day of rest.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani: Sunday is the third day after man's creation, and the third day of recovery is most painful.
Reish Lakish: an added soul is given on Shabbat and removed at its end, leaving one weakened on Sunday.
Cites Exodus 31:17 about God ceasing and resting on the seventh day.
Reads the verse's word vayinafash as vai nefesh, lamenting the soul lost when Shabbat ends.
The mishna: on Sunday they read the portions beginning with Genesis 1:1 and Genesis 1:6.
A baraita: the Creation passage is read by two people, while the firmament passage is read by one.
Asks why the Creation passage is read by two people, since it has five verses and a reader must read at least three.
Cites the mishna in Megilla that one may not read from the Torah fewer than three verses.
Rav holds that the second reader repeats a verse rather than splitting one.
Shmuel holds that the middle verse is split between the two readers.
Asks why Rav, who says to repeat a verse, did not also say to split one.
Rav holds that verses Moses did not divide may not be divided, so he does not split.
Objection to Shmuel: Rabbi Hanina said that splitting a long verse was allowed only for schoolchildren.
Shmuel answers that splitting is permitted for schoolchildren out of necessity, and here too splitting is necessary.
Asks why Shmuel did not say to repeat a verse, as Rav does.
Repetition is avoided because of decrees about people who enter or leave the synagogue mid-reading.
Objection from a baraita: a five-verse section is split between two readers, contradicting both Rav and Shmuel.
Distinguishes the two views: each view treats that baraita differently, so the cases do not conflict.

28a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that the second reader has room, meaning he may continue reading from the following paragraph.
The mishna: a long passage is read by two people in the morning, additional and afternoon services, read as the community does.
A dilemma: does the mishna mean the afternoon reading is recited by heart, or the morning reading is from a scroll and the others by heart?
Brings a baraita: in the morning and additional services they enter and read from the Torah as usual, but the afternoon reading is by heart.
Rabbi Yosei objects that one person cannot read Torah by heart before the community, so all of them read together as with Shema.
The mishna: a day with hallel but no additional offering has no non-priestly watch reading, and a day with a wood offering has no closing reading.
Asks what distinguishes days with an additional offering from days with a wood offering, and why one is Torah law and the other rabbinic.
The mishna lists the times for the wood offering of priests and the people.
A baraita asks why it was necessary to state the times for the wood offering of priests and people.
When the exiles returned, they found no wood in the Temple chamber, so these families donated wood from their own supplies.
The prophets stipulated that these families would donate their own wood on these specific days even when the chamber was full.
Cites Nehemiah 10:35 about casting lots for the wood offering at appointed times year by year.
The mishna adds that priests, Levites and others also took part in the wood offering.
A baraita asks who the descendants of those who deceived with a pestle and those who packed figs were.
Explains that the Greek kingdom decreed against bringing wood and first fruits and posted guards, as Jeroboam had done.
Asks what the worthy and sin-fearing people of that generation did in response.
They brought first fruits baskets covered with dried figs and carried them with a pestle on their shoulders.
When they reached the guards, the guards asked where they were going.
They replied they were making fig cakes at the mortar ahead, then decorated the baskets and brought them to Jerusalem.
A Sage teaches that the descendants of Salmai of Netophat did the same thing.
Asks who the descendants of Salmai of Netophat were.
Explains the Greek decree against wood, the guards on the roads, and Jeroboam's similar blockade of the pilgrim Festival.
Asks what the sin-fearing people of that generation did.
They brought their wood, made ladders, placed them on their shoulders, and went on toward Jerusalem.
When they reached the guards, the guards asked where they were going.
They replied they were fetching doves from a nearby dovecote, then took the ladders apart and brought them up to Jerusalem.
The Gemara says the verse refers to these families and to others like them.
Cites Proverbs 10:7: the memory of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked shall rot.
The mishna: on the twentieth of Av, the wood offering was brought by the descendants of Pahath Moab ben Yehuda.
A tanna identifies them as descendants of David ben Yehuda, with the name Moab from Ruth, following Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yosei says they are the descendants of Joab ben Zeruiah, whose mother descended from Ruth.
The mishna: on the twentieth of Elul, the descendants of Adin ben Yehuda brought their wood offering.
A baraita: the descendants of Adin ben Yehuda are the descendants of David ben Yehuda, according to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Yosei says that the descendants of Adin ben Yehuda are the descendants of Joab ben Zeruiah.
The mishna: on the first of Tevet, the descendants of Parosh brought wood for a second time.
Asks whose opinion the mishna follows, since it is neither Rabbi Meir's, Rabbi Yehuda's nor Rabbi Yosei's.
Works through each rabbi's view: each would have taught a different tanna's group returning a second time, so the mishna must follow another.
The mishna follows Rabbi Yosei, with two tanna'im whose views agree with him, so neither group repeated a second time.
The mishna: on the first of Tevet there was no non-priestly watch, because of the additional offering, hallel and wood offering.
Mar Kashisha son of Rav Chisda addresses Rav Ashi, introducing a question on the first of Tevet.

28b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what distinguishes hallel, which overrides its own morning watch, from the additional offering, which does not.
Rav Ashi argues a fortiori: if the offering overrides other watches, it should certainly override its own.
Rav Hisda replies that the offering should override only its own watch, not the closing prayer watch.
Rav Ashi cites Rabbi Yosei, who agrees with Rav Hisda, and brings a baraita to support him.
Rabbi Yosei's baraita: on any day with an additional offering there is a non-priestly watch.
Asks which watch Rabbi Yosei means, and whether it is the morning watch.
The first tanna also says this, so Yosei must mean another watch; the Gemara tests the afternoon and closing watches and rejects them.
Concludes that the additional offering overrides its own watch but not a watch that is not its own.
Asks why the mishna does not teach that on the first of Nisan there was no watch because of hallel, additional offering and wood offering.
Rava answers that the hallel recited on the New Moon is a custom, not required by Torah law.
Cites Rabbi Yohanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak listing the days an individual completes hallel.
Rav came to Babylonia, saw them reciting hallel on the New Moon, and concluded it was their ancestral custom.
A baraita: an individual should not begin hallel on the New Moon, but if he began he should complete it.
The mishna: five calamities befell our ancestors on the seventeenth of Tammuz, including the breaking of the tablets.
Asks from where we derive that the tablets were broken on this day.
A baraita: the Ten Commandments were given on the sixth of Sivan, though Rabbi Yosei says the seventh.
Explains that whichever date the Ten Commandments were given, Moses ascended the mountain on the seventh day of Sivan.
Cites Exodus 24:16 and 24:18 to show Moses was on the mountain for forty days and nights.
Calculates the forty days: the remaining twenty-four days of Sivan plus the first sixteen days of Tammuz.
Moses descended on the seventeenth of Tammuz and broke the tablets.
Cites Exodus 32:19 describing Moses breaking the tablets beneath the mountain, showing it happened on that day.
Explains that the nullifying of the daily offering on the seventeenth of Tammuz is a tradition.
Asks how the city's breach occurred on the seventeenth, when Jeremiah 52 seems to say the ninth.
Rava says the verses refer to different Temples: the First Temple breach was on the ninth, the Second Temple breach on the seventeenth.
The mishna: on the seventeenth of Tammuz Apostemos publicly burned a Torah scroll, which the Gemara calls a tradition.
The mishna: on the seventeenth of Tammuz Manasseh placed an idol in the Sanctuary.
Asks from where we derive that this occurred on the seventeenth of Tammuz.
Cites Daniel 12:11 about the daily offering being removed and the abomination set up, linking the idol to that day.
Asks whether only one idol was placed there, given the plural detestable things in Daniel 9:27.
Rava says two idols were placed, one fell on the other and broke its hand, so only the whole one is mentioned.

29a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: An idol tells another idol that it will give it a hand in destroying the Temple by leading Israel to worship it.
The mishna: the decree that our ancestors would not enter the Land was issued on the Ninth of Av.
Asks from where we derive this decree.
Cites Exodus 40:17 about the Tabernacle being erected on the first day of the first month of the second year.
Explains that Moses built the Tabernacle in the first year and erected it in the second, when he sent the spies.
Cites Numbers 10:11 about the cloud rising from the Tabernacle on the twentieth day of the second month.
Cites Numbers 10:33 about the people setting out from the mountain of God for three days' journey.
Rabbi Hama bar Hanina says that very day the people turned away from God by fearing to leave Mount Sinai.
Cites Numbers 11:4 about the mixed multitude lusting and the Israelites weeping.
Cites Numbers 11:20 about eating meat for a whole month.
Calculates that after three days' journey and twenty days the month of eating meat ended on the twenty-second of Sivan.
Cites Numbers 12:15 about Miriam being shut out of the camp for seven days.
Calculates that the stay in Hazeroth lasted until the twenty-ninth of Sivan, including Miriam's seven days.
Cites Numbers 13:2 about sending men to spy out the land of Canaan.
A baraita: on the twenty-ninth of Sivan Moses sent the spies.
Cites Numbers 13:25 about the spies returning after forty days, which ends on the Ninth of Av.
Asks how this works, since the remaining days of Sivan, Tammuz and Av add up to only thirty-nine.
Abaye says Tammuz that year had thirty full days, so there are exactly forty days until the Ninth of Av.
Cites Lamentations 1:15 about an appointed time called against the young men, alluding to the added day.
Cites Numbers 14:1 about the people weeping that night, which Rabbi Yohanan identifies as the Ninth of Av.
Rabba quotes Rabbi Yohanan that the night was the eve of the Ninth of Av.
God tells them they wept needlessly that night and so established a true weeping for future generations.
The mishna: the Temple was destroyed the first time on the Ninth of Av.
Cites II Kings 25 as the source for the date of the first destruction.
Quotes II Kings 25:8-9 on Nebuzaradan burning the Lord's house in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar.
Quotes Jeremiah 52:12-13 giving the tenth of Av as the date Nebuzaradan came to Jerusalem and burned the house.
A baraita reconciles the two dates: the seventh and the tenth cannot each be the sole date of burning.
Asks how the two verses can be reconciled.
Gentiles entered the Sanctuary on the seventh and eighth and desecrated it, and set it on fire on the ninth, burning all day.
Cites Jeremiah 6:4 about the shadows of evening stretching out, read as a prophecy of the burning.
Rabbi Yohanan would have set the fast on the tenth since most of the Sanctuary burned then, and the Sages reply that marking the start of the tragedy is preferable.
Asks from where we derive that the Second Temple was destroyed on this date as well.
A baraita: meritorious matters come on auspicious days and bad ones on inauspicious days, such as the Ninth of Av.
The Sages list the circumstances of the first destruction, including the Levites singing on their platform.
Asks what song the Levites were singing.
They were singing Psalms 94:23 about God bringing their iniquity upon them.
They did not finish the verse before gentiles came and conquered them, and the same happened at the second destruction.
Beitar was captured on the Ninth of Av.
The mishna: Jerusalem was plowed on the Ninth of Av.
A baraita: when Turnus Rufus plowed the Sanctuary, a decree of execution was issued against Rabban Gamliel.
A Roman officer announced in the study hall that the man with the nose is wanted, and Rabban Gamliel went into hiding.
The officer asks Rabban Gamliel privately whether, if he saves him, he will bring him into the World-to-Come.
Rabban Gamliel answers yes.
The officer asks for an oath, and Rabban Gamliel swears to him.
The officer climbed to the roof and fell to his death, and the Romans cancelled their decree, as their custom required.
A Divine Voice declares that the officer is designated for the life of the World-to-Come.
The Sages taught: when the first Temple was destroyed, young priests gathered holding the Temple keys.
The young priests went up to the roof, offered the keys to God, and threw themselves into the fire.
Isaiah lamented over them.
Quotes Isaiah 22:1-2 and 22:5, the second verse indicating that God too shouts over the destruction of the Temple.
The mishna: from the beginning of Av one decreases rejoicing.
Rav Yehuda quotes Rav that just as one decreases rejoicing when Av begins, one increases it when Adar begins.

29b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Pappa advises a Jew with litigation against a gentile to avoid him in Av, when fortune is bad, and to pursue it in Adar.
Cites Jeremiah 29:11 about giving a future and a hope, read as referring to the Babylonian exile.
Rav Yehuda quotes Rav that the verse refers to palm trees and linen garments, which last and benefit while they exist.
Cites Genesis 27:27 about the smell of Jacob's garments as the smell of a blessed field.
Rav Yehuda quotes Rav that Isaac's smell was like that of a field of apple trees.
The mishna: during the week of the Ninth of Av one may not cut hair or launder clothes.
Rav Naḥman: the prohibition covers only laundering and wearing clean clothes, so laundering to set aside is permitted.
Rav Sheshet: even laundering to set aside is prohibited.
Rav Sheshet cites the idleness of Rav's household launderers that week as proof.
Rav Hamnuna objects with a mishna that on Thursday these actions are permitted in deference to Shabbat.
Asks what the deference to Shabbat would be if laundering and wearing were permitted on Thursday.
The mishna permits laundering on Thursday for one who has only one shirt, since it is in deference to Shabbat.
Rav Asi quotes Rabbi Yohanan that one with only one shirt may launder it during the intermediate days of a Festival.
Rabbi Binyamin quotes Rabbi Elazar that laundering to set aside is permitted, and only laundering and wearing are prohibited.
A baraita prohibits laundering even to set aside until after the Ninth of Av, a conclusive refutation of Rav Naḥman.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Giyorei quotes Rabbi Yohanan that wearing linen garments is prohibited during that week.
The mishna: when the Ninth of Av falls on Shabbat, it is prohibited to be in the same week.
Rav holds the prohibition applies only before the Ninth of Av, so laundering after it is permitted.
Shmuel holds that even after the Ninth of Av laundering remains prohibited until the end of the week.
A baraita objection: the week's prohibitions are lifted on Thursday, and asks how that works when the Ninth of Av falls on Shabbat.
If the Ninth of Av is on Sunday one may launder the whole preceding week; if on Friday, one may launder on Thursday in deference to Shabbat.
If one did not launder on Thursday, one may launder on Friday from afternoon prayer onward, which Abaye and Rav Aha bar Yaakov cursed.
A baraita: if the Ninth of Av falls on Monday or Thursday, three people read from the Torah; on Tuesday or Wednesday, one reads.
Rabbi Yosei says three people always read, and one recites the Prophets portion for the Ninth of Av.
This baraita is a conclusive refutation of Shmuel's view, since it permits laundering on the weekdays after the Ninth of Av.
Shmuel could answer that this is a dispute between tannaim, so his view has tannaitic support.
A baraita: on the Ninth of Av falling on Shabbat one eats normally, and cutting hair and laundering are prohibited from the New Moon, per Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Another baraita gives the same three opinions on the period of mourning, supporting that some tannaim prohibit activities even after the fast.
Rabbi Yohanan says all three tannaim derived their views from one verse.
Cites Hosea 2:13 about God ending her mirth, her festival, her New Moon and her Shabbat.
Explains that the one who prohibits from the New Moon until after the fast is Rabbi Meir.

30a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Each opinion derives its ruling from a different word in the verse: her festival, her New Moon, or her Shabbat.
Rava rules in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and also with Rabbi Meir.
Both rulings are lenient, and both are needed so that the restrictions end on the Ninth of Av itself, as Rabbi Meir holds.
The mishna: on the eve of the Ninth of Av one may not eat two cooked dishes in one meal.
Rav Yehuda: this applies only from the sixth hour onward, so earlier in the day it is permitted.
Rav Yehuda: this applies only to the concluding meal before the fast, not to a meal one does not stop eating.
Both of Rav Yehuda's rulings are lenient, and both are needed to limit the prohibition to the concluding meal from the sixth hour.
A baraita in accordance with the second version: one who will eat another meal may eat meat and drink wine at this meal.
A baraita in accordance with the first version: on the eve of the Ninth of Av one may not eat two cooked dishes, meat, or wine.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says one must adjust and decrease the amount eaten; Rabbi Yehuda explains how.
Asks how one should adjust the meal.
Rabbi Yehuda explains: one eats only one dish, dines with half his usual company, and drinks half his usual cups, from the sixth hour onward.
Another baraita: on the eve of the Ninth of Av one may not eat two dishes, meat or wine, in Rabbi Meir's view.
The Rabbis say one must reduce meat and wine rather than abstain entirely.
Asks how one reduces his meat and wine.
One who usually eats a liter of meat eats half a liter, one who usually drinks a log of wine drinks half, and one who does not usually eat or drink them abstains.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: one who usually eats a radish or salted food after his meal may do so, as it is not an additional dish.
Another baraita: a meal eaten because of the fast forbids meat, wine and bathing, while other meals permit meat and wine but still forbid bathing.
Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei, in his father's name: bathing is permitted whenever eating meat is permitted.
A baraita: all mourning practices apply on the Ninth of Av, including eating, drinking, anointing, shoes, marital relations, and Torah study.
A mourner may read a part of Scripture he does not usually read, and study a part of Talmud he does not usually study.
Cites Psalms 19:9 about the precepts of the Lord rejoicing the heart, the reason schoolchildren stop study that day.
Rabbi Yehuda says one may not read even an unfamiliar part of Scripture, but may read Job, Lamentations and Jeremiah's prophecies of doom.
Schoolchildren interrupt their studies on that day.
Cites Psalms 19:9 as the reason schoolchildren interrupt their studies.
The mishna: one may neither eat meat nor drink wine on the eve of the Ninth of Av.
A tanna in the Tosefta: one may eat heavily salted meat and drink wine from his press, which has not finished fermenting.
Asks how long meat must remain in salt before it is permitted.
Shmuel holds that salted meat is permitted once it is more than the two days and one night of peace-offerings.
Asks until when wine is considered wine from one's press.
As long as the wine is still fermenting.
A tanna taught that fermenting wine poses no concern of exposure, and its fermenting period is three days from pressing.
Rav Yehuda quotes Rav: Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Ilai's custom was to eat stale bread with salt on the eve of the Ninth of Av.

30b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Describes a man who sits between the oven and stove eating bread and water, appearing like one whose dead relative lies before him.
The mishna: where people work on the Ninth of Av one works, where they do not one does not, while Torah scholars always rest.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says everyone should conduct himself like a Torah scholar on the Ninth of Av, so as to feel the fast.
Another baraita: one who eats and drinks on the Ninth of Av is as if he eats and drinks on Yom Kippur.
Rabbi Akiva says one who works on the Ninth of Av never sees a sign of blessing from that work.
The Sages say one who works on the Ninth of Av without mourning for Jerusalem will not see her future joy.
Cites Isaiah 66:10 about rejoicing with Jerusalem and mourning for her.
From this verse they concluded that one who mourns for Jerusalem merits seeing her joy, and one who does not does not.
A baraita: one who eats meat and drinks wine on the Ninth of Av is subject to the verse about his iniquities.
Cites Ezekiel 32:27 about iniquities upon their bones as the warning in that verse.
The mishna: Rabbi Yehuda requires overturning the bed, but the Sages do not agree with him.
The Sages ask Rabbi Yehuda what will happen to pregnant and nursing women who cannot sleep on the floor.
Rabbi Yehuda replies that he too spoke only of those able to do so.
Another baraita: Rabbi Yehuda concedes to the Sages for one unable, and the Sages concede to him for one able.
Asks what the practical difference between them is.
A baraita: overturning the bed means all the beds in the house, as Rabbi Yehuda maintains.
Rava rules that the halakha follows our mishna, and the Sages did not concede to Rabbi Yehuda at all.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says there were no days as joyous for Israel as the fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur.
Asks why Yom Kippur is joyful, as it brings pardon and was when the last tablets were given, but the fifteenth of Av needs explaining.
Asks what the special joy of the fifteenth of Av is.
Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel: it was the day tribes were permitted to intermarry with other tribes.
Asks what the basis of that teaching is in Scripture.
Cites Numbers 36:6 about the daughters of Zelophehad, which the Gemara reads as applying only to that generation.
Rav Naḥman quotes Rav Yosef: the fifteenth of Av is the day the tribe of Benjamin was readmitted to the congregation, after the oath at Mizpah.
Asks what exposition allowed them to dissolve the oath.
Rav reads the verse literally: none of us, not none of our children, so the oath bound only that generation.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana quotes Rabbi Yoḥanan: the fifteenth of Av was the day the deaths of the wilderness generation ceased.
Cites Deuteronomy 2:16-17 showing God's speech to Moses resumed only after that generation died, so the day was established for rejoicing.
Ulla says the fifteenth of Av was the day King Hoshea son of Ela canceled Jeroboam's guards on the roads to Jerusalem.

31a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The people may ascend to wherever they wish, to Jerusalem, Bethel or Dan.
Rav Mattana says the fifteenth of Av brought an additional salvation: the slain of Beitar were buried, and the blessing Who is good and does good was instituted at Yavne.
Rabba and Rav Yosef say the fifteenth of Av is when cutting wood for the altar ceased, since the sun's strength weakens and the wood would not be dry.
Rav Menashya says the day was called the breaking of the scythe, as tree cutting stopped and trees were celebrated.
Asks what the word ye'asef, he will be gathered, means in the phrase about adding Torah study.
Rav Yosef explains that it means his mother will bury him, since he is gathered to his grave.
The mishna and a baraita: the daughters of Jerusalem went out in borrowed white garments so as not to embarrass those without their own.
The mishna: all borrowed garments require immersion, and Rabbi Elazar says even folded garments stored in a box need it.
The daughters of Israel went out to dance in the vineyards, where a man without a wife could find one.
Women of distinguished lineage would invite young men to choose a wife.
A baraita describes what the beautiful, the distinguished and the plain women of Jerusalem would tell the young men.
Ulla quotes Rabbi Elazar: in the future God will sit among the righteous in Eden, arranging a dance in which each points to Him.
Cites Isaiah 25:9 about the righteous saying this is our God for whom we waited and rejoicing in His salvation.
The closing formula: the chapter concludes, the tractate Taanit is complete.
